units.title: Introductions I: Before You Start and Making Entries
units.summary: Learn what this syllabus is for, what students need before they begin, and how entries, timetables and retakes work.

sections.h: Why choose this syllabus?
p: Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language (0510) helps students understand and use English in real life. They learn to understand written and spoken English. They also learn to write and speak clearly about both familiar and less familiar topics.

Cambridge IGCSE is the most popular international qualification for 14 to 16 year olds. Students can choose from about 70 subjects. It is taught in over 4,500 schools in more than 140 countries. Universities and employers know and trust it.

b: Confident: uses a range of language to share ideas in writing and speaking.
Responsible: looks for chances to use and improve English.
Reflective: thinks about different opinions and answers politely.
Innovative: uses language in a creative way.
Engaged: tries different ways of learning and uses English in many situations.

sections.h: Before you start
p: Cambridge suggests that students have already studied an English as a Second Language course, such as the Cambridge Lower Secondary programme, or a national course at the same level. This is advice, not a rule.

The syllabus is planned for about 130 guided learning hours. Guided learning hours means the time a teacher spends teaching or guiding the student. Some students need fewer hours and some need more. It depends on local practice and on what the student already knows.

b: 130 hours over two school years is about 3 hours a week for 40 weeks each year.
A student who already speaks a lot of English at home may need fewer hours.
A student who is new to English may need extra lessons or extra practice at home.

sections.h: When can students take the exam?
p: Every Cambridge school belongs to one of six administrative zones. Each zone has its own timetable. You can see your timetable at www.cambridgeinternational.org/timetables.

Students can be entered in the June and November exam series. Schools in India can also enter students in the March series. Always check that you are using the syllabus for the year your students will take the exam. Private candidates can enter too, but only if the centre can run and mark the Speaking test and send the work to Cambridge for checking.

b: A school plans to teach for two years and finish in time for June. The students sit June.
A student who is not ready can wait and sit November.
A private candidate asks a school to help. The school must be able to record and assess the Speaking test first.

sections.h: Combining with other syllabuses and making entries
p: Students can take this syllabus together with other Cambridge syllabuses in the same exam series. There are a few exceptions. They cannot take it with Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language (0511) Count-in Speaking, IGCSE (9-1) English as a Second Language (0993 or 0991), IGCSE First Language English (0500), IGCSE (9-1) First Language English (0990), Cambridge O Level English Language (1123), Cambridge IGCSE English (as an Additional Language) (0472), or any syllabus with the same title at the same level.

Exams officers send the entries to Cambridge. Work closely with your exams officer so that the right students are entered for the right papers. Cambridge gives exams officers a Guide to Making Entries. It lists the entry option codes. The syllabus and all exam papers are in English only.

ex.t: Example: retakes and carrying marks forward
b: Students can retake the whole qualification as many times as they want.
Marks from Paper 3 Speaking can be carried forward to a later series. Check the Cambridge Handbook for the rules.
Students cannot send in a Speaking test from an earlier series again, in whole or in part.

sections.h: Teaching it in class: your first two weeks with a new group
p: The first two weeks set the tone for two years. Use them to find out where students are and to show them what the course will feel like. In lesson 1, tell students in simple words what the exam is: three papers (Reading and Writing, Listening, Speaking), what each paper looks like, and how marks are earned. Show one real exercise from a past paper so that the exam does not feel like a mystery.

In lessons 2 to 4, run a short diagnostic of all four skills. For Reading, give one past-paper reading exercise. For Writing, ask for a 120 to 160 word email. For Listening, play one short extract with five multiple-choice questions. For Speaking, hold a five-minute conversation with each student, or with pairs, using everyday topics such as food, travel or technology. Do not give grades. Write a short note for each student: one strength, one need for each skill.

In lesson 5, give each student a one-page learner profile. It lists their four strengths and four needs and one goal for the term, written together with you. File it. Return to it every half term. Students who can see their own progress are more responsible and more engaged, which matches two of the Cambridge learner attributes.

b: Name and class. Date.
Reading: strength (finds facts quickly); need (misses implied meaning). Writing: strength (clear ideas); need (few linking words).
Listening: strength (gets names and numbers); need (loses track in long talks). Speaking: strength (fluent); need (short answers, little expansion).
Goal for this term: use three linking words in every piece of writing and expand every speaking answer with a reason and an example.

sections.h: Common difficulties for second-language learners, and what to do
p: Students in your class share a mother tongue or speak several languages at home. This is a strength, but it also shapes their English. Typical problems are: pronouncing sounds that do not exist in their home languages, using the wrong word stress, leaving out word endings such as -s and -ed, mixing up articles (a, an, the), and translating word for word from the home language so that a sentence sounds strange in English. Expect these errors. They are normal and they can be improved with practice.

Many students are also afraid of speaking in case they make mistakes. Build a classroom where mistakes are welcome. Praise the attempt first, correct one important error at a time, and use pair work so that students can try ideas in private before they speak to the class. Many students read slowly because they try to understand every word. Teach skimming, scanning and guessing from context so that they can cope with texts of 400 to 650 words in the time allowed.

Finally, students often write what they would say, not what the task needs. They forget the purpose, the reader and the format. This is why every writing lesson should start with three questions: Why am I writing? Who will read it? What type of text is it?

ex.t: Example: quick fixes you can use tomorrow
b: Word endings: ask students to underline every verb in their writing and check the ending.
Articles: collect ten sentences with a/an/the errors and let the class fix them together.
Stress: say words in a clap pattern (PHOto, phoTOgraphy) so students feel the stress.
Fear of speaking: use 30-second pair talks before any whole-class speaking.

sections.h: Teacher self-check: am I ready to start?
p: Use this list at the end of the unit. Tick what you can already do and plan how to learn the rest. You should be able to: explain the three papers and their marks to a parent in two minutes; name the sixteen skills (R1 to R4, W1 to W4, L1 to L4, S1 to S4); say when the exam series are and who the exams officer is; explain what a guided learning hour is and how many are planned; and say how Speaking is reported.

You should also know where the Cambridge papers, mark schemes and examiner reports are found and where the school's entry deadlines are published. If you cannot answer one of these questions, go back to the section above or ask your exams officer. A Cambridge teacher does not need to remember every number, but must know where to find it and must check it each year.

b: How many marks is Paper 1 and how long is it?
Which paper is marked by the teacher and checked by Cambridge?
Which grade scale is used for Speaking?
What are the guided learning hours?
Who can I ask about entries and access arrangements?

units.activity: Write a one-page plan for your school. Include: how many guided learning hours you have, which exam series you will use, who your exams officer is, and the date you will talk to them about entries. Check the timetable for your zone first.

check.q: About how many guided learning hours does the syllabus plan for?
Who sends the entries to Cambridge?

units.title: Implementing the Cambridge Curriculum: Planning, the Pathway and How to Teach
units.summary: Understand what a curriculum is, the twelve principles behind a good Cambridge curriculum, the Cambridge Pathway, how to timetable it, and the teaching approaches of a Cambridge teacher.

sections.h: Introduction: why this unit matters
p: Cambridge International gives schools a rich menu, not one fixed recipe. It says that the most important work in designing and running a curriculum is done by a school's own leaders and teachers. You make the programme fit your students, your culture and your school's values.

This unit is based on the Cambridge guide 'Implementing the Curriculum with Cambridge'. It is written for school leaders, but teachers need it too, because teachers turn the plan into real lessons. When you finish, you should be able to explain what a curriculum is, describe the Cambridge Pathway, plan time for English as a Second Language, and teach in the way Cambridge hopes its teachers will.
Take your time. This is a long unit. Read one part, think about your own school, and make notes. You will use these ideas in Week 3 when you plan your own year.

b: Part 1: What a curriculum is, and 12 principles of a good one.
Part 2: The Cambridge Pathway, English language options, timetabling and different school systems.
Part 3: The Cambridge teacher, learner attributes, reflection, collaboration and technology.

sections.h: 1.1 What is a curriculum?
p: The word curriculum is used in different ways around the world. Some countries use it in a wide sense. It includes the subjects, the links between them, the way teachers teach and every part of school life that shapes a learner's experience. Other countries use it in a narrow sense: only a list of courses or only one learning programme.

Cambridge uses four simple definitions. The school curriculum is the whole combination of subjects a learner studies in a school year and in the years that follow. A subject curriculum is the content and skills in one syllabus, spread over stages of learning. The co-curricular curriculum is the valued activities outside lessons that the school supports, such as clubs, sport and music. The experienced curriculum is what learners really receive, including the planned and unplanned results of school life.

ex.t: Example: the four curricula in one school
b: School curriculum: English, Mathematics, Science, History and ESL each year.
Subject curriculum: the IGCSE ESL (0510) syllabus.
Co-curricular: debate club, school newspaper, drama.
Experienced: what a student really learns, including from a kind teacher or an unkind comment in the corridor.

sections.h: 1.1 continued: the wider learning experience
p: A good school gives more than the sum of its subjects. Learning does not begin or end in the classroom. It is in the school environment and in the community. What learners really experience can differ from what is written down, because many things work together: the school's vision and values, the quality of teaching, what learners already know, how motivated they are, school leadership and culture, the subject curricula, assessment habits, and the school's internal structures.

This is why every school's experienced curriculum is different. It also means schools should check regularly whether the experience matches their intentions. A simple way for you to do this in your own classroom is to ask students at the end of a unit: What helped you most? What was confusing? What would you change?

b: Ask: 'What is one thing you learned this week that was not on my plan?'
Collect answers on paper without names.
Read them. This shows you the experienced curriculum in your classroom.

sections.h: School vision, mission and plan, and the planning questions
p: A school vision is a clear picture of where the school wants to go. It should inspire the whole school community and be widely shared. A mission statement says the school's purpose. Together with the aims, these give focus. The school strategic plan then turns the vision into actions, usually with priorities for up to five years and a detailed plan for the next year.

Cambridge lists many questions that a school should answer when it plans its curriculum. For learners: What are the expected academic, personal and social outcomes? Which skills should learners gain? How will the curriculum motivate and challenge them? For teachers: Which teaching and assessment practices are central? What professional development is needed? For structure: Which Cambridge programmes will the school use? How will it support learners who do not have English as a first language? How many hours for each subject? Will learners have choice? What facilities and money are needed?

ex.t: Example: questions an ESL department can ask
b: What English level do our students have when they join?
How many hours a week can we give to ESL?
Which staff have Cambridge training, and who needs it?
What rooms and equipment do we need for Listening and Speaking?
How will we check that our students are really learning?

sections.h: 1.2 Twelve principles for a successful curriculum (Part 1: principles 1 to 4)
p: Cambridge believes twelve principles are important in every school. Principle 1: the school curriculum should be broad, balanced and consistent, with clear and smooth progression for all learners. This means the school's values and aims must guide decisions. Quality matters more than quantity: too much content leaves no time for deep understanding. Progression must be steady. Learning should use a spiral approach, where each stage returns to key ideas and builds on them. Balance usually includes mathematics, languages, sciences, technology, humanities, creative arts and physical education. Schools must also plan how to combine Cambridge with other programmes, and must write their own schemes of work, because the curriculum is built locally.

Principle 2: the instructional system should be well aligned and coherent. Curriculum, pedagogy (how we teach) and assessment must fit together and support each other. Cambridge syllabuses, teacher support, endorsed textbooks and professional development are designed to be aligned. Principle 3: the curriculum should develop learners and teachers who are confident, responsible, reflective, innovative and engaged. Principle 4: each subject curriculum should give learners and teachers inspiring, relevant content, with the right breadth and depth, arranged in a learning spiral so that each year builds on the last and learners revisit key skills in new contexts.

ex.t: Example: a learning spiral in ESL
b: Year 1: write a short informal email with three paragraphs.
Later: write the same text type with more detail and a wider range of linking words.
Final year: write it under time limits, with a clear purpose and reader, and with few errors.
The text type returns, but the standard rises each time.

sections.h: 1.2 continued: principles 5 to 8
p: Principle 5: the curriculum should recognise each learner's language background and give the support they need to reach the curriculum. All Cambridge qualifications are assessed in English, so learners need enough English to take the exams. Schools should also keep developing each learner's first language, because it supports thinking, identity and international understanding. Cambridge suggests that all teachers become language aware: they plan language support in their lessons and act as language teachers of their own subject. Cambridge also supports bilingual education and the method called CLIL (content and language integrated learning). Examiners use a positive marking approach: they award marks when a learner shows understanding, and learners are not penalised for spelling and grammar except in tests of language skills.

Principle 6: assessment has several purposes. Assessment for learning gives feedback during learning. Summative assessment judges the standard reached at the end of a period. Many Cambridge assessments are high stakes. Principle 7: clear and meaningful standards are needed to measure progress and allow fair international comparison. Principle 8: teachers are the most powerful influence on student learning. Teachers make the curriculum real by turning aims into lessons, so teachers should also show the learner attributes. Continuous professional development and reflective practice are essential, and Cambridge encourages experienced teachers to become trainers and examiners.

ex.t: Example: being a language-aware teacher (also in other subjects)
b: Pre-teach five key words before a reading.
Use sentence starters, such as 'One cause of this is...'.
Let students discuss in pairs before they write.
Give feedback on ideas first and on language second.

sections.h: 1.2 continued: principles 9 to 12
p: Principle 9: to get the best results with Cambridge curricula, learners must be actively engaged. Knowledge cannot be passed from teacher to learner like a parcel. Learners build understanding in their own minds. Teachers must listen to the learner's voice in class and in written work, and must challenge the learner's ideas. Teachers lead learning; they do not only facilitate it. They keep checking the effect of their teaching and change it using feedback.

Principle 10: strong leadership is needed for lasting school improvement. Good leaders create conditions for teachers to succeed, and teachers can lead too. Principle 11: curriculum development is an ongoing process of gathering and using evidence. Schools should review their curriculum regularly, ask 'Is it delivering what it intends? How do we know? What do students think?' and then refine the plan. Principle 12: the curriculum must help all learners reach their potential. Effective schools are those that move all students forward, whatever their starting point.

ex.t: Self-check: which principle helps me most this term?
b: Principle 9 if my lessons are too teacher-talk.
Principle 5 if some students struggle with English in other subjects.
Principle 11 if I have never collected feedback from students.
Write one action for the principle you chose.

sections.h: 2.1 The Cambridge Pathway
p: The Cambridge Pathway has four stages, shown in the picture below. Cambridge Primary is for ages 5 to 11, Cambridge Lower Secondary for 11 to 14, Cambridge Upper Secondary for 14 to 16, and Cambridge Advanced for 16 to 19. Age ranges are for guidance only. Each stage builds on the one before. Cambridge Professional Development supports teachers and school leaders at every stage.

Three ideas are important. First, there is a difference between the written Cambridge programme (the syllabus and documents) and the taught curriculum in your school. Teachers can add local content and case studies, so that the curriculum reflects national culture and heritage. Second, Cambridge qualifications are set at three levels. The end of Upper Secondary (IGCSE or O Level) gives an international standard and opens the way to AS and A Level or other university preparation courses. In some countries students can enter university foundation programmes directly with IGCSE. Third, no school has to use the whole Pathway. Schools can choose some stages, or combine Cambridge with national programmes.

b: Primary and Lower Secondary: English as a second language is a separate subject with its own curriculum framework.
Upper Secondary: IGCSE English as a Second Language (0510), and also Cambridge IGCSE English as a first language for stronger speakers.
Advanced: students can choose AS and A Level English subjects, and some universities ask for proof of English.

sections.h: 2.2 Cambridge Primary
p: Cambridge Primary is for learners aged 5 to 11. It has curriculum frameworks in 10 subjects, including English, English as a second language, Mathematics, Science and Cambridge Global Perspectives. Each framework has six stages, normally taught one stage a year, but schools can use shorter or longer periods. No subject is compulsory, so schools choose what fits their learners. The frameworks are divided into strands. For English, the strands include reading, writing, and speaking and listening.

There are two testing options. Progression Tests are used whenever the teacher feels the class is ready, from stage 3 to stage 6, and are marked by the teacher. Primary Checkpoint is at the end of the Primary programme. Cambridge marks it and gives feedback on strengths and weaknesses. It covers English, English as a second language, mathematics and science.

Cambridge Primary English as a second language prepares learners to be skilled users of English for practical purposes, including using English to learn other subjects. It is based on the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) and is built for speakers of other first languages.

b: If your students come from a Cambridge Primary school, ask for their Checkpoint report. It shows their strengths and weaknesses.
If they do not, use your own diagnostic test (see Week 3).
Do not repeat what students already know; build on it.

sections.h: 2.3 Cambridge Lower Secondary
p: Cambridge Lower Secondary is for learners aged 11 to 14. It builds on Primary and prepares learners for Upper Secondary. It is a three-stage programme with frameworks in the same subjects as Primary. Again, no part is compulsory. Cambridge regularly reviews each framework to make sure learners are ready for the next stage.

Cambridge Lower Secondary English as a Second Language continues from the primary curriculum and develops independent users of English at levels B1 and B2 on the CEFR. It gives learners the English skills they need to access Cambridge Upper Secondary qualifications through English, and learners can continue to Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language. There are Progression Tests for each stage, and the Lower Secondary Checkpoint at the end of the stage. Cambridge marks the Checkpoint tests for English, English as a second language, mathematics and science.

Students joining your IGCSE class from a Cambridge Lower Secondary course should have worked on all four skills, so they already know the idea of reading for specific information and of writing for different readers.

ex.t: Example: a student arrives with a Lower Secondary Checkpoint report
b: The report says: strong reading, weaker writing.
Plan: more writing practice in your first term, with models and feedback.
Check progress with your own test after six weeks.

sections.h: 2.4 Cambridge Upper Secondary
p: Cambridge Upper Secondary (ages 14 to 16) offers over 70 IGCSE subjects and over 40 O Level subjects. IGCSE stands for International General Certificate of Secondary Education. Schools can offer almost any combination, and each subject is certificated separately. An IGCSE is the formal recognition of a learner's achievement at the end of a course. Its content is made to suit many schools and to avoid cultural bias. Grades are A* to G (and 9 to 1 for some subjects and zones). In the UK it is accepted as equivalent to the GCSE. Some IGCSE subjects have optional coursework. O Level is similar but graded A* to E, and is not available in administrative zones 1, 2 and 6.

Some IGCSE subjects have a core curriculum and an extended (supplement) curriculum, called tiering. In these subjects students take either core, with grades C to G, or core and extended, with grades A* to G. Streaming students into a tier changes their future options, so schools should decide carefully, and may provide extra support so more students can reach the extended material. IMPORTANT: the 2024 to 2026 IGCSE English as a Second Language (0510, Speaking Endorsement) syllabus that you are studying removed tiers. All candidates take the same papers. Always check the syllabus for your exam year.

Learners usually study IGCSE in one or two years, and a few schools use three years or 18 months. Some schools allow very able learners to take an exam a year early. About 130 hours of teaching are planned for each IGCSE subject. Some subjects have barred combinations: learners cannot take both in the same exam series, for example two overlapping English language syllabuses.

b: IGCSE: over 70 subjects, A* to G, about 130 guided learning hours.
O Level: over 40 subjects, A* to E.
ESL 0510 2024 to 2026: no tiers. Always check the year of your syllabus.
Barred combinations: check your syllabus and the Handbook before entering students.

sections.h: 2.5 Cambridge Advanced
p: Cambridge Advanced (ages 16 to 19) is for learners who want to specialise. It includes Cambridge International AS and A Level (over 50 subjects), Cambridge Pre-U (in the UK), the AICE Diploma and Global Perspectives & Research. An AS Level has half the content of an A Level. It can be taken alone after one year, or as the first half of an A Level. A Level grades are A* to E and are in standard with UK A Levels. Cambridge Pre-U is available in the UK, and schools outside the UK need special approval.

There are three approaches to planning AS and A Level. Approach 1: a non-staged route in which learners take all A Level papers at the end of the second year. Approach 2: a staged route in which learners take AS in year 1 and/or year 2, then complete the A Level at the end. Approach 3: AS Level only, which gives a broader but less specialised programme. Schools should check the requirements of the universities their learners want to join. Teachers will need more teaching time and independent study time for each subject at this level: about 180 hours for AS and 360 hours for A Level, including directed study.

ex.t: Why ESL teachers should know this
b: Many of your students will go on to AS and A Level. Their IGCSE English results affect their choices.
Some universities ask for IGCSE ESL, others for IGCSE First Language English or a test such as IELTS.
Ask your students' counsellor what their target universities require.

sections.h: 2.6 Alternative approaches to English language development and showing English proficiency
p: Cambridge offers English in several ways. Cambridge International offers English as a school subject, with pathways for first-language learners, bilingual learners and second-language learners. Its sister organisation, Cambridge Assessment English (Cambridge English), offers English language qualifications that universities, governments and employers accept worldwide. Both reference the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR), which describes language ability on a six-point scale from A1 (beginner) to C2 (mastery). This makes it easy to compare qualifications.

Cambridge International English as a Second Language is made for schools where part or all of the curriculum is taught in English. It runs through the Pathway from Primary to Upper Secondary and fits with the rest of the Cambridge curriculum. Learning objectives are organised into five strands: Use of English, Reading, Writing, Speaking and Listening. IGCSE ESL aims to build skills in listening, speaking, reading and writing so learners become independent users of English, able to communicate in practical situations. The Cambridge English programmes for schools are often best where English is the only subject taught in English and where close CEFR alignment is a high priority.

Students who plan to study in English-speaking countries must meet university language rules. Some universities accept a good grade in IGCSE English as a Second Language, while others require IGCSE First Language English. In the UK, some courses require a Secure English Language Test (SELT), such as IELTS. Make sure students and parents know the rules early.

ex.t: Example: the CEFR levels in plain words
b: A1 and A2: basic user (simple everyday sentences).
B1 and B2: independent user (can deal with most situations and explain opinions).
C1 and C2: proficient user (fluent and precise).
In the 0510 syllabus: grade C overall with Speaking grade 2 can be seen as about B2.

sections.h: 2.7 Timetabling the curriculum
p: After designing the curriculum, schools must make a timetable. The timetable depends on many things: the length of the school day, days per week and year, how much choice learners have, co-curricular activities, extra courses without exams (such as religious studies or student leadership), multi-levelling (different year groups in one class), and setting by ability. It also depends on limits: the number of teachers and support staff, their contracts and experience, classrooms and special rooms such as laboratories, and money for resources and language support.

Cambridge gives suggested guided learning hours. Primary English and English as a second language: 120 to 150 hours a year (about 4 to 5 hours a week). Lower Secondary English and ESL: also 120 to 150 hours a year. Upper Secondary: about 130 hours per IGCSE or O Level subject before the assessments. Advanced: about 180 hours for an AS Level and a further 180 for an A Level (non-staged: 360 hours over two years). The hours include teaching time and directed study, but not independent study.

The length of a lesson changes teaching. Short periods can become mostly whole-class talking. Longer lessons are wasted if the teacher has not prepared enough varied activities. In one example school, the day has nine 40-minute periods. Older learners have double periods of 80 minutes, so each subject gets four hours and 40 minutes per week. Teachers should plan several different activities that together meet the aims of the syllabus.

b: How many ESL lessons a week do you have? How long is each?
Multiply by the number of real teaching weeks to find your hours per year.
Compare with about 130 hours for the whole course.
If you are short, ask what can change: more lessons, homework, clubs or extra support.

sections.h: 2.8 Teaching Cambridge in systems with different school years
p: The Cambridge Pathway has 13 stages and usually one stage is covered per year. But some countries have 12 years of school, or start school later, or compress stages. Schools can teach programmes over a different length of time, as Cambridge programmes are designed to be flexible. Most schools teach IGCSE in two years, in grades 10 and 11 (when students are about 16), and some offer it over 18 months. Typically, students then take AS Levels in grade 11 or 12 and A Levels in grade 12 or 13.

The guide gives case studies. In Southern Africa, schools have 12 years, so IGCSE is taught in grades 10 and 11, and AS and A Level in the last years. Some schools speed up: Lower Secondary starts a year early in grade 7. In Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, schools must deliver 13 stages in 12 years. One structure compresses stages 7 to 9 into two years: stage 7 and half of stage 8 in grade 7, and the rest of stage 8 and stage 9 in grade 8. In India, a school covered Cambridge Primary in five years by moving some stages earlier. A school in Beijing taught IGCSE in one year, in about nine months, with eight English lessons a week. A school in Brunei used vertical option blocks to widen choice.

ex.t: What this means for an ESL teacher
b: If your school compresses the Pathway, plan carefully so that no important language skill is skipped.
Check your students' ages and stage when you read Checkpoint results.
If time is short, give priority to the skills the exam assesses and to the language students need to learn other subjects.

sections.h: 2.9 Curriculum models for bilingual and multilingual schools
p: Many schools use Cambridge for the English-medium part of a bilingual or multilingual programme, and use the national curriculum for the first-language part. The right model depends on the school's vision, staff, resources and how much students hear English outside school. Models differ in how long they last (short or long term) and how strong they are (low or high intensity). A school might start small by teaching one module in English. Another might immerse students in English for a short time. A third might teach one or two subjects in English for years. A fourth might teach a large part of the curriculum in English over many years.

Bilingual education usually means meeting two curricula. Approach A is the split curriculum: some subjects follow the national curriculum in the first language, and other subjects follow the international curriculum in English, so there is no double timetable. This only works if both qualifications are officially recognised. Approach B is the shared subject curriculum: some subjects are taught in both languages. It can use an integrated curriculum (a teacher or team teachers compare the two curricula, find the overlap and teach once, perhaps rotating between languages across weeks or years) or two separate curricula (separate classes with no mapping, which is easier to organise but may repeat content).

Cambridge recommends CLIL as a method: teachers support students in learning the language they need for the subject. Schools will need a training plan so local teachers can build their English and teach in English. Even when a school is not bilingual, a good language policy and language awareness in every subject help students. In one case study, a school in the Netherlands requires all students in its bilingual programme to take IGCSE English as a Second Language and Global Perspectives. ESL is taught in regular English lessons, and the IGCSE helps show that students have reached CEFR B2.

ex.t: Example: curriculum mapping for one subject
b: List the topics in the national curriculum.
List the topics in the Cambridge syllabus.
Mark the overlap and the differences.
Teach the overlap once and teach the differences separately.

sections.h: 3.1 The Cambridge teacher
p: Excellent teaching, including developing the learner attributes, is the biggest influence a school has on learners' results and personal growth. There is no single recipe for excellent teaching, and different cultures have strong traditions that should be respected. But research shows some practices help learners. Understanding is built in the learner's mind. Teachers must listen to the learner's voice, in class and in work, and use it to challenge and extend what the learner thinks. This helps learners become independent.

The most effective teaching challenges learners beyond what they can do alone. Vygotsky called the area just beyond a learner's independent ability the zone of proximal development. Teachers support, or scaffold, learning in that zone. Cambridge calls this approach active learning: learners are active, not passive, and teachers lead learning actively, not just give information or only facilitate. Teachers should use a variety of strategies: individual tasks, group work and whole-class teaching that includes discussion. Teachers should use assessment often to check whether learners are reaching the aims and to help learners see where they are and how to improve.

b: Show a model email and ask students what makes it good.
Give a plan frame with the three prompts.
Let students write the first paragraph in pairs.
Take away the support: they write the second and third paragraphs alone.
Give feedback and repeat with less support next time.

sections.h: 3.1 continued: teachers as role models
p: Outstanding teachers show the Cambridge learner attributes themselves. They have mastery of their subject and can relate its ideas and skills so learners understand what the subject is about. They teach for understanding and not only coverage, and they revisit key ideas in different contexts (a spiral). They connect learning to the real world and to other subjects. They scaffold learning. They have a learning orientation rather than a performance orientation: they care that students learn well, not just look good. They model problem solving and take care of the whole development of the learner, including attitudes, emotions and confidence.

They understand and can use assessment for different purposes. They use a variety of teaching strategies and activities. They are reflective and creative practitioners who keep learning. They are collaborative and supportive of colleagues and the school community. Cambridge also publishes Cambridge Teacher Standards to help teachers and schools see what good practice looks like and plan development.

b: I know my subject well and can explain it simply.
I teach for understanding, not just to finish the book.
I connect lessons to students' real lives.
I use assessment to help students, not only to give marks.
I learn from colleagues and share ideas.

sections.h: 3.2 The Cambridge learner and teacher attributes
p: Schools want learners who understand their own culture and nation, and also have the skills to be global learners. Cambridge's five attributes aim to build five learning habits. Confident: learners work with ideas and information in a structured, critical way, and can defend their views and respect those of others. Teachers are confident in their subject and show a love of learning. Responsible: learners take ownership of their learning, set targets, act with integrity and support others. Teachers are highly professional and care about the whole development of each student.

Reflective: learners understand themselves as learners, think about both the process and the product of learning, and develop strategies for life-long learning. Teachers reflect on their practice through research, evaluation and adaptation. Innovative: learners welcome new challenges, solve unfamiliar problems and adapt flexibly. Teachers are creative, try new ideas and techniques and are flexible. Engaged: learners are intellectually, socially and professionally ready to make a difference. Teachers are passionate about learning in and beyond the classroom and share their knowledge with the wider community. The attributes are not complete: schools can add their own. They need to be supported in lessons and in co-curricular life, and all school staff should help.

ex.t: Example: showing an attribute in an ESL lesson
b: Confident: every student speaks for one minute each lesson.
Responsible: students set a weekly vocabulary target.
Reflective: students write one sentence on what helped them learn.
Innovative: students write a story using five new words.
Engaged: students share an English article with the class.

sections.h: 3.3 Becoming a reflective learner
p: Reflection means thinking about your own learning and judging your progress accurately. Reflective learners plan and manage their work, understand themselves as learners, use strategies to overcome difficulties, learn from mistakes and see failure as a chance to learn. They are emotionally strong when things go wrong. They are confident but not arrogant, and they know that learning is social and shared with others. Becoming reflective also needs the other four attributes: confidence, responsibility, innovation and engagement. All the attributes are connected.

Many schools assume learners will become reflective alone. This is not enough. All teachers should help students learn how to learn. Separate 'study skills' classes tend not to work well, because learning strategies are best built in real lessons. A passive learner who re-reads notes again and again believes that understanding can be poured into memory. An effective learner knows that learning is active: asking questions, finding the barrier, trying a plan and checking if it works. To support this, schools should state clear aims, build the language of learning, build links between subjects, and give teachers professional development and professional learning communities.

ex.t: Example: a reflection routine for ESL students (5 minutes)
b: What did I do well in this task?
What was hard, and why?
What will I do differently next time?
Which skill (R, W, L or S) did I practise?
Keep the answers in a learning log and review it every month.

sections.h: 3.4 Disciplinary and interdisciplinary approaches
p: Schools build the curriculum around a balance of subjects (disciplines), because each subject develops ways of thinking that are hard to get from everyday life. Michael Young calls this 'powerful knowledge'. But subjects overlap, and learners should also see the connections. Understanding a subject well is the foundation for good interdisciplinary work; without it, learning becomes shallow. Interdisciplinary understanding means you can move between subjects, make connections and see the whole picture.

Schools can support this by expecting teachers to plan together. A simple example: the mathematics teacher teaches statistics, and the geography teacher makes students use those statistics in coursework. In ESL, you can connect with science by teaching how to write a report on an experiment, or with history by teaching how to write an article about an event. Cambridge Global Perspectives is an interdisciplinary programme offered from Primary to A Level. It teaches students to evaluate evidence and arguments, to understand other perspectives and to do research and teamwork. It can be taught as a separate subject or used as the core of the curriculum.

ex.t: Example: ESL working with other subjects
b: Science: write an experiment report with linking words for cause and effect.
Geography: write a formal report on a local issue.
History: write an article describing an event for a school magazine.
Ask a colleague what texts students must write in their subject and teach the language for them.

sections.h: 3.5 Using conceptual frameworks to support learning
p: Concepts are ways of grouping ideas to make sense of a complicated world. They give us a shared language to understand and act. Each subject uses many concepts. Substantive concepts are part of the content, for example in geography: river, trade, city, ecosystem. Second-order concepts shape the key questions of a subject, for example in history: cause and consequence, change and continuity, similarity and difference. Some concepts appear in more than one subject, such as 'renewable energy' in science, geography, economics and politics, or 'change'.

A threshold concept is one that, once understood, changes how learners understand a field and helps them move to the next level (Meyer and Land, 2003). Part of good teaching and planning is deciding which concepts are most important at each stage. Cambridge syllabuses help by identifying important concepts, but teachers adapt them to their own lessons. Key concepts help students link topics, review and apply knowledge, and think like a skilled mathematician, historian or chemist. For example, in economics, 'opportunity cost' links many topics. Cambridge has a 'Getting started with Key Concepts' guide for more help.

ex.t: Example: key concepts for ESL (a teaching suggestion, not an official list)
b: Purpose and audience: who am I writing or speaking to, and why?
Register: formal and informal language.
Cohesion: how ideas are linked with linking words and reference words.
Stated and implied meaning: what is said and what is suggested.
Plan your lessons so these concepts come back in Reading, Writing, Listening and Speaking.

sections.h: 3.6 Collaboration
p: Students need to work well as team members and leaders, because this is important in life and at work. They also need to solve problems together. The OECD (2013) describes collaborative problem solving as the capacity of a person to take part effectively in a process where two or more people try to solve a problem by sharing understanding and effort and by pooling their knowledge, skills and efforts to reach a solution.

Collaboration needs groups to work with a shared goal, with everyone taking responsibility. Roles can change as the work moves on. Students need to define the problem, make sure they share the same understanding, think critically as a group and reflect on how well the group is progressing. Collaboration is not the same as cooperation, and teachers should know the difference when they plan group work. Schools can build collaboration through fieldwork, science practicals, project work and courses like Cambridge Global Perspectives, and through clubs and other co-curricular activities.

b: Groups of four plan a class magazine.
Roles: editor, writer, designer, speaker.
They agree the goal, divide the work, write in English, check each other's text and present.
At the end, they reflect: What worked? What would we change?

sections.h: 3.7 Information literacy and using ICT in the classroom
p: Using ICT well is an essential skill for all learners. Computers, laptops, tablets and smartphones are used in classrooms all over the world, and learners use them to find, process, judge and share information and data. Including ICT can be hard, but it is vital. The key rule is that technology must support carefully planned teaching and learning goals. It should not replace them. For example, a teacher who uses an interactive whiteboard so that the whole class is actively involved is using ICT well. Using it only as another way to lecture is not.

With so much information online, information literacy is very important. It means more than knowing how to find information. It means thinking critically about it and judging its meaning and reliability. Information literacy should be at the heart of every subject and of interdisciplinary work, as it is in Cambridge Global Perspectives. Cambridge also offers professional development qualifications on using ICT in classrooms.

ex.t: Ideas for ESL teachers (suggestions, always check school and exam rules)
b: Use audio and video to give students more listening practice and to model pronunciation.
Let students record themselves speaking and listen again to improve.
Teach students to check an online source: Who wrote it? When? Is there evidence?
Remember: dictionaries and devices are not allowed in the exam, so also practise without them.

sections.h: Bringing it together: your action plan
p: You have now seen how Cambridge thinks about curriculum, pathway, time, language and teaching. Use this to write a short action plan for your own school. Choose one idea from each part and write what you will do, when, and how you will know it worked. For example: 'I will add a five-minute reflection to every writing lesson by the end of this month, and read students' answers each Friday.'

Share your plan with a colleague or your head of department. Ask for one suggestion. Keep the plan, because in Week 3 you will build a full year plan and a diagnostic test, and this plan will help you.

b: Curriculum: one thing I will check or change (for example, hours for ESL).
Pathway: one thing I will find out (for example, what my students learned in Lower Secondary).
Teaching: one teaching habit I will start (for example, scaffolding).
Attributes: one attribute I will build in my students and how.
Date to review: ____.

units.title: Introductions II: Accessibility, After the Exam and Using the Grades
units.summary: Understand access arrangements, how grades and results are reported, and how teachers and students can use the grades.

sections.h: Accessibility and equality: fair for all students
p: Cambridge tries to make its syllabuses and exam papers fair for students of every country, culture and background. The language and layout of papers are planned to be as easy to access as possible. This helps all students show what they know.

Even so, some students need extra help. Cambridge uses access arrangements for students with special educational needs (SEN), a disability, an illness or an injury. These follow the idea of reasonable adjustments in the UK Equality Act (2010). They remove barriers without making the exam easier.

ex.t: Example: who might need an access arrangement?
b: A student with a hearing problem may need a different way to take the Listening test.
A student with a broken writing arm may need help with writing.
A student with a reading difficulty may need a modified paper.

sections.h: Rules for access arrangements
p: Access arrangements must be based on evidence that the student faces a barrier. They should also match the way the student normally works at school. Cambridge must agree that the arrangement is a reasonable adjustment, has a reasonable cost and time, and does not harm the security of the exam.

Check what is available at the start of the course, not just before the exam. Read the Cambridge Handbook at www.cambridgeinternational.org/eoguide. If you need something that is not on the standard list, contact Cambridge early. A student who cannot access part of the assessment may still receive an award based on the parts they completed.

b: In week one of the course, note any students who may need help.
Collect evidence, such as notes from teachers or reports.
Ask your exams officer to check the Handbook and apply on time.

sections.h: After the exam: grades and results
p: Students receive grades A*, A, B, C, D, E, F or G. A* is the highest and G is the lowest. Ungraded means the work did not reach the standard for grade G. Ungraded appears on the statement of results but not on the certificate.

Speaking is reported separately. Where students reach the right standard, the certificate shows a Speaking grade from 1 (high) to 5 (low). The Speaking marks do not change the written grade. Sometimes the statement of results shows Q (pending) or X (no result). These letters do not appear on the certificate. The certificate names the qualification as International General Certificate of Secondary Education (IGCSE).

b: Grade B in written papers and Speaking grade 2: two separate results on one certificate.
Grade C overall with Speaking grade 2: Cambridge says this can be seen as about level B2 on the Common European Framework (CEFR).
Q means the result is pending. X means no result.

sections.h: How students and teachers can use the grades
p: Assessment has two purposes. First, it measures learning and achievement. It confirms how well a student has shown the knowledge, understanding and skills in the syllabus. Second, it shows likely future success. Results help to predict who is well prepared for a course or a job. They help students choose the best course or career.

Teachers can use results to improve teaching. Look at which skills were strong and which were weak. Ask which papers need more practice next year. Cambridge gives teachers results analysis and examiner reports for this.

ex.t: Example: using results in a staff meeting
b: Listening results were lower than Reading. Plan more listening practice.
Many students lost marks on the formal writing task. Teach register and format.
Share the examiner report with colleagues and agree two actions.

sections.h: Inclusion in the classroom, before any access arrangement
p: Access arrangements for the exam are only part of inclusion. Good teaching for all students starts in the classroom. Use clear fonts and enough space on handouts. Give instructions in short steps and both say them and write them. Check understanding by asking students to repeat the task in their own words. Seat students who find it hard to hear or see near the front. Give time to think before you ask for an answer. Allow quiet students to share ideas in writing or pairs first.

Remember the rule from Cambridge: an access arrangement should reflect the student's normal way of working at school. That means that if a student will need extra time or a reader in the exam, you must already be giving that kind of support in lessons and tests, and you must keep notes about it. Do not wait until the last month. Talk to your head of department, SENCO or exams officer at the start of the course. Keep a simple file for each student with the barrier, the support you give and the evidence.

b: Date, student, barrier seen (for example, slow reading speed).
Support used in class or test (extra reading time, large print).
Result (finished task, scores improved).
Who was told (parent, exams officer).

sections.h: Using results to improve your teaching
p: When results arrive, treat them as information, not as a verdict. Cambridge provides a Candidate Results Service, Results Analysis and Principal Examiner Reports for teachers. Use Results Analysis to compare how your students performed on each paper and each skill. Look for patterns: Was Listening much weaker than Reading? Did most students score low on the formal writing task? Did Speaking marks match your own internal marks?

Then make a plan. For each weak area choose one change and one date. For example: 'Add ten minutes of Exercise 3 listening every Monday' or 'Teach register in week 3 of next term and mark every Exercise 6 with the Content and Language tables'. Share the plan with your department and review it after the next set of mock exams. This is how teachers improve results year after year.

ex.t: Example: a results meeting in 30 minutes
b: 5 minutes: read the headline results for each paper.
10 minutes: find the weakest skill and the weakest exercise.
10 minutes: choose two teaching changes and who will do them.
5 minutes: write the actions and the review date in the department plan.

sections.h: Talking to students and parents about grades
p: Parents and students often ask, 'What does this grade mean?' Prepare a short, honest answer. A* to C means students are well prepared for a wide range of courses. Grade C overall with Speaking grade 2 can be seen as roughly B2 on the CEFR. Cambridge IGCSEs are accepted by leading universities and employers. Never promise a grade. Say what the student can do now and what must improve to reach the next step.

Use simple language and examples. For example: 'Tolu is very good at finding facts in a text, but she loses marks in the formal writing task because her paragraphs are not linked. If she practises linking words and writes one practice review every week, she can improve.' Always end with an action that the student and the parent can help with.

ex.t: Example: a three-sentence report to parents
b: Strength: reads and listens well, gets most multiple-choice items right.
Need: writing lacks detail and organisation, which affects the Language mark.
Next step: one 120 to 160 word practice text each week, marked with the Content and Language tables.

units.activity: Choose one student (or an imaginary one) and write two lines for each: (1) an access arrangement that might help and the evidence you would collect, and (2) how you would explain the student's grade and Speaking grade to the parent.

units.title: Syllabus Overview: Aims, Content, Assessment and Objectives
units.summary: See the big picture: the aims, what students learn, how the three papers fit together, and the sixteen skills that earn marks.

sections.h: Aims: what the course is for
p: The aims describe the purpose of any course based on this syllabus. The aims are to: develop students' ability to use English well for practical communication; develop their awareness of the nature of language and of how to learn languages; develop skills that help in other subjects; and support their personal development and enjoyment.
Keep these four aims on your wall. When you plan a lesson, ask: will this help the student use English in real life?

b: Practical communication: students leave a voice message to book a doctor's visit.
Awareness of language: students notice how a polite email differs from a text to a friend.
Transferable skills: students plan and present a short talk they can also use in Science.
Enjoyment: students choose a topic they care about for a speaking task.

sections.h: Content overview
p: The course builds practical skills in reading, writing, listening and speaking. Students read many kinds of text. They learn to pick out the right details, to tell what is stated from what is only suggested, and to write for different purposes and readers.

Students listen to talks and conversations. They speak about many topics and learn to answer in a way that fits the situation and the listener, with good accuracy and clarity. By the end, they should be independent users of English for further study and for daily life.

b: Topic: protecting the environment.
Reading: an article about plastic waste.
Writing: an email to a friend about a clean-up day.
Listening: a radio interview with a volunteer.
Speaking: a short talk on how to reduce waste at home.

sections.h: Assessment overview: three papers
p: Every student takes three components and can receive grades A* to G. Paper 1 is Reading and Writing. It takes 2 hours, has 60 marks and is 70 per cent of the written grade. It has six exercises: four reading and two writing. It is marked by Cambridge.

Paper 2 is Listening. It takes about 50 minutes, has 40 marks and is 30 per cent. It has five exercises and is multiple choice. It is marked by Cambridge. Paper 3 is Speaking. It takes about 10 to 15 minutes and has 40 marks. It is an interview, a short talk and a discussion. The teacher marks it and Cambridge checks the marks. Speaking is separately endorsed: it does not change the written grade.

ex.t: Example: the numbers at a glance
b: Paper 1: 2 hours, 60 marks, 70%.
Paper 2: about 50 minutes, 40 marks, 30%.
Paper 3: about 10 to 15 minutes, 40 marks, separately endorsed (grade 1 to 5).
There are no tiers in this version of the syllabus: all students take the same papers.

sections.h: Assessment objectives: the sixteen skills
p: Assessment objectives (AOs) are the skills the exam rewards. AO1 Reading: R1 understand specific facts; R2 understand how ideas, opinions and attitudes connect; R3 pick out details for a purpose; R4 understand implied meaning. AO2 Writing: W1 communicate information, ideas and opinions; W2 organise ideas with linking words; W3 use a range of grammar and vocabulary; W4 use the right register and style for the purpose and reader.

AO3 Listening: L1 specific information; L2 speakers' ideas, opinions and attitudes; L3 connections between them; L4 what is implied but not said. AO4 Speaking: S1 communicate ideas, facts and opinions; S2 control a range of vocabulary and grammar; S3 develop answers and keep talking; S4 control pronunciation and intonation. Weighting of the whole qualification: Reading 35 per cent, Writing 35 per cent, Listening 30 per cent. Speaking is separately endorsed. Inside Paper 1, Reading and Writing are 50 per cent each.

b: 'When does the festival start?' is R1 (a stated fact).
'What does the writer suggest about the town?' is R4 (implied meaning).
An informal email to a friend tests W4 (register) as well as W1 to W3.
Tell students the skill name before they practise. It helps them know what to do.

sections.h: The sixteen skills in plain classroom words
p: Turn each assessment objective into a sentence that students understand. Reading. R1: I can find the facts the text gives me. R2: I can see how ideas, opinions and feelings connect (for example, because, but, so). R3: I can choose the right details for a purpose. R4: I can understand what the writer means but does not say. Writing. W1: I can give facts, ideas and opinions clearly. W2: I can put ideas in order and join them with linking words. W3: I can use a range of grammar and vocabulary. W4: I can write in the right style for the reader.

Listening. L1: I can catch specific information such as names, times and places. L2: I can understand what speakers think and feel. L3: I can follow how their ideas link. L4: I can understand what is hinted but not said. Speaking. S1: I can talk about ideas, facts and opinions. S2: I can use a range of words and grammar and control them. S3: I can develop my answers and keep the conversation going. S4: I can say words clearly and use stress and intonation to show meaning.

Print this list for your students. Ask them to colour each skill green, yellow or red every month. Seeing the skills as small, learnable abilities helps students feel that the exam can be improved step by step.

b: Put the sixteen 'I can' sentences on the classroom wall.
After a task, students write the skill code on a sticky note to show which skill they practised.
Review the wall each month: which skills have many notes and which have none?

sections.h: Weightings and how they should shape your teaching time
p: Reading is 35 per cent of the written grade, Writing 35 per cent and Listening 30 per cent. Speaking is separately endorsed, but it is a compulsory component. If you have about 130 hours, a rough guide for planning might be: about 45 hours for Reading skills, about 45 hours for Writing, about 40 hours for Listening, and speaking practice built into almost every lesson. This is only a guide. Adjust it to your students' needs.

Remember that Writing earns its marks from two things at once: Content (6) and Language (9) in each task. A student who writes a relevant but simple text may earn most of the Content marks and few of the Language marks. This is why you should plan regular practice in vocabulary range, sentence variety and linking, not only in 'what to write'. In Reading and Listening, remember that every question is worth one mark, so students should answer every question and not leave blanks.

ex.t: Example: a term plan using the weightings
b: Weeks 1 to 4: reading skills (skim, scan, careful reading) plus paragraph linking in writing.
Weeks 5 to 8: listening exercises 1 and 2 plus informal email writing.
Weeks 9 to 12: listening exercises 3 to 5 plus review writing and a speaking mock.

sections.h: Common misunderstandings about the syllabus
p: 'Speaking does not count.' Speaking does not change the written grade, but it is a separate result on the certificate and it is compulsory. Employers and universities read it, so teach it seriously. 'The exam is only about grammar.' The exam tests how well students understand and communicate in English, not how well they recite rules. 'More words get more marks.' Writing tasks are marked for relevance, development and control of language, not length. Students who go far above the word range can lose control and accuracy.

'We can use any old past paper.' Always use papers for the right syllabus and the right year, and check the Changes section. The 2024 to 2026 syllabus removed tiers, replaced the summary task with a multiple-choice question, made Listening 100 per cent multiple choice, and increased the Speaking marks from 30 to 40. Older papers may not match. 'Any dictionary can be used.' Dictionaries are not allowed in Paper 1 or Paper 3.

ex.t: Example: myth or fact? A staff meeting game
b: Read each statement above aloud.
Teachers vote 'myth' or 'fact' with coloured cards.
Check the syllabus pages together and discuss why the myth is attractive.

check.q: What share of the written grade is Paper 1 Reading and Writing?
Which objective is about understanding what is implied but not directly stated in a text?

o: Separately endorsed with its own grade

units.title: Subject Content: Reading, Writing, Listening and Speaking
units.summary: See what students should be able to do in each skill, with clear examples and the text types they meet.

sections.h: Reading: what students learn to do
p: Students meet many kinds of text: instructions, notices, advertisements, leaflets, articles, blogs, reviews and web pages. The texts can describe, tell a story, give information, persuade, discuss or argue. Students should read widely in English, in class and at home.

They learn to find facts, to follow ideas, opinions and attitudes and the links between them, to understand what is implied, and to choose the right details for a purpose. They also learn reading strategies: skim reading (read fast to get the general idea), scanning (look for specific information) and careful reading (read slowly to understand detail). Good readers predict answers and notice what type of information a question wants.

ex.t: Example: three ways to read one blog post
b: Skim: read the title and the first line of each paragraph to learn what the post is about.
Scan: look for the date and the price when a question asks 'when' and 'how much'.
Read carefully: read the paragraph about the writer's feelings to answer an opinion question.
Guess a new word: read the sentences around it and decide what it probably means.

sections.h: Writing: what students learn to do
p: Students write for different purposes and different readers. They learn the features of each text type and are encouraged to plan, draft and check their work. They communicate facts, ideas and arguments clearly and add detail. They show control of grammar, vocabulary, punctuation and spelling.

They organise ideas in a logical order with paragraphs and linking words. For cause and effect they use words like therefore, because of, as a result and consequently. For adding ideas they use in addition, moreover and furthermore. For contrast they use however, in contrast, whereas and although. They use a range of grammar and vocabulary, such as different tenses, conditionals, phrasal verbs, collocations and idioms, and they avoid repeating the same word. They also choose the right register: informal for an email to a friend, more formal for a report, essay, review or article.

b: Informal (to a friend): 'Hi Sam! Guess what, I'm coming to your town next week. Fancy meeting up?'
Formal (to a teacher): 'Dear Mr Banda, I would like to ask whether I may hand in my essay on Friday.'
Teach students to ask: who is reading this and why am I writing?

sections.h: Listening: what students learn to do
p: Students listen to phone messages, announcements, radio programmes, TV, film, plays, news items, podcasts, conversations and interviews. These can be formal, semi-formal or informal. Students should listen to English widely in class and at home.

They learn to catch factual details such as places, names, times, dates and directions. They learn to understand speakers' ideas, feelings and attitudes, and the reasons behind them. They notice link words and pronouns. They work out what is implied and guess unknown words from the words around them. Before listening, they predict the type of information they will hear.

ex.t: Example: before, during and after listening
b: Before: read the question and decide if you need a name, a number, a place or a feeling.
During: write nothing long; listen for the key word and the link words such as but, so and because.
After: check that your answer matches what the speaker meant, not just a word you heard.

sections.h: Speaking: what students learn to do
p: Students speak in different situations: asking and answering in class, short exchanges, conversations, giving opinions and short talks. They practise functional language such as expressing preferences, telling a personal story, describing an experience, agreeing and disagreeing, giving advantages and disadvantages, and making predictions. Topics are everyday: the environment, health, food, film, travel, technology, celebrations, science, the arts and shopping.

They learn to expand answers by giving examples ('just to name a few'), giving reasons ('and that is why'), comparing ('just like', 'while'), speculating ('I suppose') and clarifying ('Sorry, I did not quite catch that'). They link ideas with discourse markers such as in addition, first of all, finally, that's why, however and although. They use a range of grammar and vocabulary and they paraphrase when they forget a word. They also work on pronunciation: word stress, sentence stress and rising and falling intonation.

b: Short: 'I like football.'
Expanded: 'I really like football, just like most of my friends. First of all, it keeps me fit, and that is why I play twice a week. However, I do not enjoy it when it rains.'
Teach students to add an example, a reason and a contrast.

sections.h: Glossary of text types
p: Article: a text for a general audience, for example in a magazine or newspaper, that informs or entertains. Blog: a text published on a website, usually informal. Conversation: a spoken exchange between two or more people, usually informal. Dialogue: any spoken exchange between two people. Email: electronic writing for a particular purpose, formal or informal. Essay: a text on a topic that gives an argument or point of view, with an introduction, main body and conclusion, and reasons or examples.

Instructions: a written or spoken text that tells you how to do something. Interview: a spoken exchange in which one person asks questions and the others answer. Leaflet: an informational text that explains or advertises something and is handed out. Monologue: a text spoken by one person only. Notice: a short written text with news or information, usually put on a wall or noticeboard. Report: a text for a superior or a group about an event, experience or situation, with facts and suggestions or recommendations. Review: a text for a general audience that describes and gives opinions about something the writer has experienced.

ex.t: Example: match the need to the text type
b: You want to tell a head teacher what happened at a school trip and suggest changes: report.
You want to give your opinion on a film you saw: review.
You want to tell a friend your news in a friendly way: informal email.
You want to inform people about a school event on a wall: notice.

sections.h: Phrase banks you can give to your students
p: Students need a toolbox of language. Use the lists in the syllabus as a base. Linking words for cause and effect: therefore, because of, as a result, consequently. For addition: in addition, moreover, furthermore, as well as. For contrast and concession: however, in contrast, whereas, although. For time and sequence in speaking: at the start of, first of all, finally. Other discourse markers: that's why, on top of that, plus, having said that.

Expansion phrases from the speaking content: to give examples, 'just to name a few'; to give a reason, 'and that is why'; to compare, 'just like', 'while'; to speculate, 'I suppose'; to clarify, 'Sorry, when you said ..., did you mean ...?' and 'Sorry, I didn't quite catch that.' Add useful phrases for opinions (in my opinion, personally), agreeing and disagreeing (I see what you mean, but ...), advantages and disadvantages, and predictions (I think it will ...).

Print the phrase bank, but do not let students simply copy it. Ask them to use at least three new phrases in each writing task and each speaking practice, and to highlight them. Over time, students move these phrases from the page into their own natural language.

b: Basic: 'I like swimming. It is good for health.'
Better: 'I like swimming because it keeps me fit. In addition, it helps me relax.'
Best: 'Although I do not have much free time, I try to swim twice a week, because it keeps me fit. In addition, it helps me relax after school.'

sections.h: Teaching vocabulary and grammar for range and accuracy
p: The Language marks reward range and accuracy. Teach vocabulary in groups, not in long lists: words that go together (collocations such as 'make a decision', 'do research'), phrasal verbs (take up, look into, find out), set phrases and a few idioms, and synonyms to avoid repeating the same word. Teach each new item with a sentence, a sentence of the student's own, and a short speaking use. Keep a class 'word wall' by topic: environment, health, food, film, travel, technology, celebrations, science, arts and shopping.

For grammar, teach a range of verb forms and tenses, conditional forms and a variety of sentence structures. Teach them through use: show a short model text, ask students to find the structure, practise it in a controlled task, then use it in a free task. For example, teach the first conditional through a short talk about an event ('If the weather is bad, we will ...') and then use it in an informal email. Mark the structure, not only the error, so that students learn what to aim for.

b: Show five new words on the board with a picture or example.
Students write one true sentence with each word.
Pairs swap and correct each other's sentences.
Next lesson, start with a quick quiz and use two of the words in a speaking task.

sections.h: A weekly timetable that builds all four skills
p: It is easy to teach only what feels comfortable. A weekly timetable stops this. If you have about four lessons a week, you might plan: Lesson 1 Reading (a short text, strategy practice, then marking), Lesson 2 Writing (plan, draft, check, with a model), Lesson 3 Listening (before-during-after, with transcript review), Lesson 4 Speaking and language (pair and group work, pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar).

Add short routines to every lesson: five minutes of vocabulary at the start, two minutes of pronunciation, and a one-minute reflection at the end ('What did I learn? What do I still find hard?'). Once a month, do a full past-paper exercise under timed conditions. Every half term, carry out a short mock of one paper. Keep a record of marks so that you can see progress.

b: Mon: Reading, skim and scan an article, then Exercise 1 style questions.
Tue: Writing, plan and write an informal email, peer-check for linking words.
Thu: Listening, Exercise 2 style extracts, check with the transcript.
Fri: Speaking, short talks in pairs, then feedback on one pronunciation point.

units.activity: Pick one topic (for example 'technology'). For that topic, write one reading task, one writing task, one listening idea and one speaking question. For each, name the text type from the glossary and the skill (R, W, L or S) it practises.

check.q: Which reading strategy means looking quickly for specific information?
Which linking word shows contrast?
