units.title: Details of the Assessment: Paper 1, Paper 2 and Paper 3
units.summary: Walk through every exercise in the three papers: what students do, how many marks, and how Speaking is run and marked.

sections.h: Paper 1: Reading and Writing
p: Paper 1 is a written paper. It takes 2 hours and has 60 marks. It has six exercises: four reading and two writing. Students answer every question. Students write on the question paper. Dictionaries are not allowed. Reading uses multiple-choice, matching and some short answers in English.

Exercise 1 (8 marks): read a text of about 400 to 450 words. Five questions need one answer and the last needs three. Answers are single words or phrases. Exercise 2 (9 marks): multiple matching. Read a text of about 600 to 650 words in up to five sections, or up to five shorter texts, and match nine questions to the right section. Exercise 3 (7 marks): read about 400 to 500 words and complete brief notes. Exercise 4 (6 marks): read about 550 to 600 words and answer six multiple-choice questions with three options A, B or C.

ex.t: Example: reading marks at a glance
b: Exercise 1: 8 marks. Exercise 2: 9 marks. Exercise 3: 7 marks. Exercise 4: 6 marks.
Total for reading: 30 marks.
Skills tested: R1, R2 and R3 in all four exercises, with R4 in Exercises 2 and 4.

sections.h: Paper 1: the two writing exercises
p: Exercise 5 (15 marks) is an informal email. Exercise 6 (15 marks) is a more formal piece, such as an article, report, essay or review. In each, students write 120 to 160 words of continuous prose. They answer a short stimulus, which may include a picture, and short prompts. The stimulus tells them the purpose, format and reader, and these are different each time.

Each writing exercise is marked out of 15: up to 6 marks for Content (doing the task and developing ideas) and up to 9 marks for Language (range, accuracy and organisation). The skills tested are W1 to W4.

ex.t: Example: what to teach for the writing tasks
b: Read the task and underline the purpose, the reader and every prompt.
Plan three short points before writing.
Write 120 to 160 words: not much shorter, not much longer.
Check grammar, spelling and linking words in the last two minutes.

sections.h: Paper 2: Listening
p: Paper 2 takes about 50 minutes, including 6 minutes to copy answers onto a separate answer sheet. It has 40 marks and 40 multiple-choice questions in five exercises. Students hear every recording twice. Check the Cambridge Handbook for the year of the exam: it explains how to get the audio and how to set up the room, equipment and sound.

Exercise 1 (8 marks): eight short extracts, one question each, with four picture options A to D. Exercise 2 (10 marks): five short extracts, two questions each, with three written options. Exercise 3 (8 marks): one monologue (for example a talk) and eight sentences to complete with a word or short phrase from three options. Exercise 4 (6 marks): six short monologues in a multiple-matching task with eight statements to choose from. Exercise 5 (8 marks): an interview between two speakers and eight multiple-choice questions.

ex.t: Example: listening marks at a glance
b: Exercise 1: 8. Exercise 2: 10. Exercise 3: 8. Exercise 4: 6. Exercise 5: 8.
Total: 40 marks.
Skills tested: L1, L2 and L3 in all exercises, and L4 in Exercises 2, 4 and 5.

sections.h: Paper 3: Speaking
p: The Speaking test is about 10 to 15 minutes and is worth 40 marks. It is in English and must be recorded in full for every student. Dictionaries are not allowed. The teacher or examiner chooses one Speaking Assessment card for each student. The teacher conducts and marks the test, and Cambridge checks (moderates) the marks.

The test has five parts. Introduction (about 1 minute): start the recording, say your name, the student's number and name and the date, welcome the student and read the script. Not assessed. Warm-up (1 to 2 minutes): a short friendly chat. Not assessed. Part 1 Interview (2 to 3 minutes): a short interview on a topic. Assessed. Part 2 Short talk (3 to 4 minutes, with 1 minute to prepare): the student reads the card, prepares without writing notes, then talks alone. Assessed. Part 3 Discussion (3 to 4 minutes): questions linked to the Part 2 topic. Assessed.

b: Introduction and warm-up put the student at ease. They earn no marks.
Interview, short talk and discussion are the three assessed parts.
The student receives a card only for Part 2. The questions for Parts 1 and 3 are in the teacher's notes.
The whole test, from the start of the introduction to the end of Part 3, must be recorded.

sections.h: Marking Speaking, moderation and sending marks
p: Speaking is marked out of 40 on four criteria, each out of 10: grammar, vocabulary, development and pronunciation. Add the four marks for the total. The marks come from level descriptions from Level 5 (9 to 10 marks) down to Level 1 (1 to 2 marks), with 0 for no creditable response. Choose the best-fit level first. If the work convincingly meets the level, give the top mark. If it adequately meets it, give a middle mark. If it only just meets it, give the lowest mark.

Record marks on the Speaking Examination Summary Form, which you download each year from the samples database at www.cambridgeinternational.org/samples. The marks on the form must be the same as the marks you send. If more than one teacher marks Speaking in your school, you must standardise (internally moderate) the marking so that every student is judged to the same standard. Cambridge then externally moderates: you send the marks of all students and a sample of the marked work. Moderators write a short report with feedback for your centre.

b: Level 5: answers are relevant and consistently well developed; the student keeps talking with ease.
Level 4: answers are relevant and mostly developed; the student keeps talking with only a little support.
Level 3: answers are relevant with attempts at development; frequent support is needed.
Use the descriptors, not your feeling, to decide.

sections.h: Exercise-by-exercise strategy for Paper 1
p: Share these strategies with students, and let them adapt them. Exercise 1 (8 marks, short answers): read the questions first; underline the question word; scan for the answer; write a few words, not a sentence. Exercise 2 (9 marks, matching): read the statements first, then read each text and mark clues; remember each letter can be used more than once; look for the idea, not the same words. Exercise 3 (7 marks, notes): look at the headings; find the right part of the text; write short notes in your own or the text's words; do not put an answer under the wrong heading.

Exercise 4 (6 marks, multiple choice): read the question, find the part of the text, then test each option; rule out options that use the same words but change the meaning. Exercise 5 (15 marks, informal email): underline purpose, reader and prompts; plan three paragraphs; use a friendly style; give details; check linking words and verb forms. Exercise 6 (15 marks, formal text): same steps but with a more formal style, a clear opening and closing, and a structure suited to the text type (review, report, essay or article).

ex.t: Example: a time plan for the 2 hours (suggestion, not an official rule)
b: About 60 minutes for the four reading exercises (60 marks across the paper means about 2 minutes per mark).
About 25 minutes for each writing task, including planning and checking.
Keep 5 to 10 minutes for a final check of all answers. Practise this plan in mocks and adjust it for each student.

sections.h: Exam skills for Paper 2 Listening
p: Paper 2 is about 50 minutes and includes 6 minutes to copy answers onto the answer sheet. Teach students to use any time given before each exercise to read the questions and guess what kind of information they will hear. In Exercise 1 the options are pictures, so students should look at the differences between pictures. In Exercises 2, 3 and 5 the options are written, so students should underline the key words in each option. In Exercise 4, students must match speakers to eight statements, with two statements not used, so they should cross out each statement after using it.

Because each recording plays twice, advise students to answer on the first listening and check on the second. They must answer every question, since a blank earns no mark. Teach them to listen for opinion words such as 'I'd rather', 'unfortunately', 'actually', 'in fact' and for linking words such as 'but', 'so' and 'although', which often show the real answer. At the end, they should transfer answers carefully: copy the right letter to the right question number.

ex.t: Example: a classroom routine for listening
b: Predict: read the questions and guess the type of answer.
Listen once: answer what you are sure of.
Listen twice: check and fill gaps.
Review: replay the extract with the transcript and underline the words that gave the answer.

sections.h: Paper 3 Speaking: what students need to know
p: Prepare students for the whole test. After a short warm-up they will answer questions in Part 1 (interview), give a short talk in Part 2, and discuss related questions in Part 3. In Part 2 they have up to one minute to read the card and prepare, but they may not write notes. Teach them to use the minute to choose three ideas in their head, to decide how to start, and to think of one example.

Teach them to keep talking: use expansion (give a reason and an example), paraphrase if they forget a word, and use phrases such as 'Sorry, could you say that again?' if they do not understand. Practise often with a timer. Record students and let them listen to themselves. This helps with pronunciation and intonation, which together carry 10 of the 40 marks.

b: Second 0 to 10: read the card, find the topic and the three bullet points.
Second 10 to 40: think of one idea and one example for each point.
Second 40 to 60: think of an opening sentence and a closing sentence.
Then speak for the time allowed, without notes.

units.title: Planning Your Two-Year 0510 Programme
units.summary: Turn the syllabus into a working plan: a two-year scheme of work, a weekly pattern, a mock-exam calendar and a progress record.

sections.h: From syllabus to scheme of work
p: A scheme of work is a map of what you will teach and when. Cambridge provides example schemes of work and teacher guides on the School Support Hub for many syllabuses. Use them as a starting point, but make your own plan for your students, your timetable and your exam series. Start with three facts: how many guided learning hours you have (about 130 is the planning figure), which exam series you will enter, and how many teaching weeks you really have after holidays, tests and school events.

Next, split the time across the four skills using the weightings as a guide. Plan the order of topics so that skills build. Early in the course teach strategies (skimming, scanning, planning an email, listening for specific information). In the middle, practise each exercise type. Near the end, run timed full papers and focus revision on weaknesses. Build speaking and vocabulary into every lesson, not only into 'speaking lessons'.

b: Series: June of Year 11. Start: September of Year 10.
Teaching weeks: about 60 over two years after holidays and school events.
Hours: about 130 guided learning hours, so a little over 2 hours a week on average.
Mock exams: end of Year 10 and in January and March of Year 11.

sections.h: A sample two-year outline
p: Year 10, Term 1: baseline tests; reading strategies (skim, scan, careful reading); paragraphing and linking words; informal email writing; Exercise 1 and 3 style short answers and notes; listening Exercise 1; speaking interview Part 1 topics (family, hobbies, school). Year 10, Term 2: Exercise 2 matching and Exercise 4 multiple choice; formal writing (review and report); listening Exercises 2 and 3; short talks (Part 2) with one-minute preparation. Year 10, Term 3: article and essay writing; listening Exercises 4 and 5; discussion (Part 3); first full practice papers; mock exam at the end of the year.

Year 11, Term 1: full past papers in sections; targeted work on the weakest skills; more advanced vocabulary and grammar for range; speaking practice with recording. Year 11, Term 2: mock exams for all three papers, marking and analysis; individual support plans; speaking practice tests with another teacher as examiner. Year 11, Term 3: final revision based on the mock results; exam technique; keep confidence high; check exam arrangements, entries and access arrangements.

ex.t: Example: weekly pattern inside the outline
b: One reading lesson, one writing lesson, one listening lesson, one speaking and language lesson.
Five minutes of vocabulary at the start of each lesson.
One full past-paper exercise each month; one half-paper each half term.

sections.h: Mock exams and the assessment calendar
p: Plan mock exams early. A mock is not only a test; it is information. Use real past papers from the right syllabus (2024 to 2026 for this course). Run Paper 1 in 2 hours without dictionaries, Paper 2 with the recording played twice, and Paper 3 as a recorded Speaking test marked with the syllabus criteria. Keep exam conditions: silence, no phones, no talking.

After each mock, mark with the mark schemes, record marks by exercise (not only the total), and write a short report for each student: strongest skill, weakest skill, and two targets. Hold a mock results meeting with colleagues, and plan reteaching for the weakest exercises. Share a simple summary with parents so that they know how to support.

b: September: baseline tests of all four skills.
December: short test of reading and writing.
March: mock Paper 1 and Paper 2.
April: mock Paper 3 (Speaking), recorded and marked.
May: final targeted revision and exam conditions practice.

sections.h: Tracking progress with a simple record
p: Keep a single sheet (paper or spreadsheet) for each class. Columns: student name, baseline marks (Reading, Writing, Listening, Speaking), then the marks for each test by exercise. Add a column for 'target skill' and 'action'. At a glance you will see which students are stuck on Exercise 3, who is strong in Reading but weak in Listening, and whose writing Language mark is low.

Review the sheet every half term. Choose the three skills with the lowest class average and the five students who need most help. Plan small-group sessions for them. Share their progress with them: students who see the chart and understand their targets are more motivated, which matches the Cambridge learner attributes of being responsible and engaged.

ex.t: Example: columns for a progress sheet
b: Name | Baseline R/W/L/S | Test 1 Ex1 Ex2 Ex3 Ex4 Ex5 Ex6 | Paper 2 total | Speaking mock | Target | Action | Review date.

units.activity: Draw up your own two-year outline using the planning facts for your school: start date, series, teaching weeks, hours and mock dates. Mark on it when you will teach each exercise of Paper 1 and Paper 2, when Speaking practice starts and when you will run your first mock. Share it with your head of department for feedback.

o: Students' ages, favourite colours, school fees
Grade boundaries, student names, parents' jobs
Guided learning hours, exam series, real teaching weeks
Cost of books, size of classroom, number of desks

o: To give grades to the exams office
To get information about strengths and weaknesses

o: It shows which skills and exercises need reteaching

units.title: Becoming a Cambridge Educator: Support, Training and Professional Habits
units.summary: Find the support Cambridge gives teachers, choose professional development, and build the daily habits of a confident Cambridge teacher.

sections.h: Where to find support
p: Cambridge International provides support in four stages. Planning and preparation: Next Steps guides, schemes of work, specimen papers, syllabuses and teacher guides. Teaching and assessment: endorsed resources, online forums, and support for coursework and Speaking tests. Learning and revision: example candidate responses, past papers and mark schemes, and specimen paper answers. Results: the Candidate Results Service, Principal Examiner Reports for teachers and Results Analysis.

The School Support Hub is the secure online site for Cambridge teachers. Ask your school's exams officer how your school gets access. You can also join discussion forums and keep up with the global Cambridge community. Sign up for email notifications about syllabus changes at the Cambridge website so that you hear about new or revised products and services.

ex.t: Example: your first week on the Hub
b: Download the syllabus and the specimen papers for 0510.
Find the scheme of work and the teacher guide.
Download one past paper, its mark scheme and its examiner report.
Join one discussion forum and read three questions from other teachers.

sections.h: Professional development routes
p: Cambridge supports teachers through Introductory Training, Extension Training and Enrichment Professional Development, each available face to face or online, and through Cambridge Professional Development Qualifications. Introductory training helps new teachers understand the syllabus and assessment. Extension training goes deeper into particular skills or assessment (for example listening, speaking, marking workshops). Enrichment courses build specific skills that can change classroom practice.

Choose a route that matches your stage. If you are new, start with introductory training. After a year of teaching the syllabus, choose extension training that matches your weakest area, for example Speaking or assessment. Keep a record of what you complete, with dates, certificates and a one-paragraph reflection on what you changed in your teaching. This record is valuable for your school and for future applications, such as becoming an examiner or moderator.

b: Year 1: introductory training, read the syllabus twice, attend one department standardisation meeting.
Year 2: extension training in the weakest skill, begin marking mocks with the full mark scheme.
Year 3: share what you learned in a staff session, support a new colleague.

sections.h: The Cambridge learner, and what it means in your classroom
p: The syllabus describes five Cambridge learner attributes. A confident learner uses a range of language to communicate ideas and information effectively in writing and speaking. A responsible learner seeks opportunities to use and develop their language skills. A reflective learner considers different opinions and information in written or spoken form and responds appropriately. An innovative learner uses language creatively to express ideas and information. An engaged learner develops different learning strategies and uses language skills in a range of situations.

Turn these into classroom habits. Confidence: give every student speaking time every lesson. Responsibility: set reading and listening homework that students choose from a list. Reflection: end every lesson with a one-sentence reflection. Innovation: allow creative tasks, such as writing a blog or recording a short podcast. Engagement: teach several learning strategies, such as keeping a vocabulary notebook, using flashcards and recording yourself speaking.

ex.t: Example: one habit for each attribute
b: Confident: every student speaks for one minute in pairs.
Responsible: students keep an 'English outside class' log.
Reflective: exit ticket, 'One thing I learned, one thing I find hard'.
Innovative: students write a short story or blog using this week's grammar.
Engaged: students choose between three study methods and report which worked.

sections.h: Professional habits: reflection, exam integrity and teamwork
p: Reflect after each unit: what worked, what did not, what I will change. Observe colleagues and invite them to observe you; ask for one strength and one suggestion. Join or start a department group to share resources and standardise marking. Keep your own copies of the syllabus, specimen papers, mark schemes and examiner reports and update them each year.

Protect the integrity of the exam. Follow the Cambridge Handbook for the year: it explains how to store and use exam materials, how to run the exam, and how to conduct and record the Speaking test. Never share live exam materials or help candidates in the exam beyond what is allowed. Remember that Speaking marks are checked by Cambridge, and moderators give feedback to your centre, so mark honestly and keep recordings safe and in good quality.

b: Week 1: read one section of an examiner report.
Week 2: observe a colleague for 20 minutes.
Week 3: mark a sample of scripts with a colleague and compare.
Week 4: write a short reflection and one action.

units.title: Assessing the Syllabus: How Marks Are Awarded
units.summary: Learn the six marking principles examiners follow, and how to read a mark scheme so you mark the same way Cambridge does.

sections.h: Why teachers need the mark scheme
p: A mark scheme shows how examiners were told to give marks. It is published to help teachers and students understand what the exam asks for. It does not show every discussion examiners had about other acceptable answers, so read it together with the question paper and the Principal Examiner's Report for Teachers.

In this week you will use real June 2024 papers: Paper 1 (0510/11) and Paper 2 (0510/21). You will learn to mark like an examiner. Then you will use the same skills to give better feedback to your students.

b: Question paper: shows what students must do.
Mark scheme: shows which answers earn marks.
Examiner's report: explains what students did well and badly and gives advice for next time.

sections.h: The six generic marking principles
p: Principle 1: marks follow the mark scheme or level descriptors, the skills named in them, and the standard shown in the standardisation scripts. Principle 2: marks are always whole marks. There are no half marks.

Principle 3: marks are given positively. Examiners give marks for correct and valid answers, and for what students clearly show they know and can do. Marks are not taken away for errors or for leaving things out. Spelling, punctuation and grammar are judged only where the question tests them, but the meaning must always be clear.

Principle 4: rules are used the same way for every script. Principle 5: use the full range of marks when students' work deserves it. Principle 6: marks come only from the mark scheme. Do not think about grade boundaries or grade descriptions while marking.

b: A student writes 'sharing a car' where the key says 'sharing a car': mark given.
A student's English has small spelling mistakes in a short answer but the meaning is clear: mark still given.
A student leaves one bullet empty: no mark for that bullet, but no mark is taken from the other bullets.

sections.h: Reading the answer column
p: For short-answer questions, a word or phrase in brackets ( ) may be written but is not needed. For example the key for Question 1 is '(19)84'. A student who writes '84' or '1984' gets the mark. Where the key shows a slash, such as 'taking photographs / selling photographs / charge for photographs', any one of these ideas earns the mark.

For questions with several marks, the key often says 'award one mark for each detail up to a maximum of three marks.' This means a student cannot score more than three, even if they write five correct things. For multiple-choice and matching questions, there is one correct letter.

ex.t: Example: what the notes in a key mean
b: Brackets ( ): can be included, not essential.
Slash /: alternative acceptable answers.
'Up to a maximum of 4 marks': stop counting at four.
'Award one mark for each detail': mark each idea separately.

sections.h: Level descriptors and best fit (for writing and speaking)
p: Writing is marked with level descriptors, not a list of answers. First read the whole script. Then decide which level statement is the best fit. Real work does not always match one level exactly, so you may need to choose between two levels.

Then choose the mark inside the level. If the work convincingly meets the level, give the top mark. If it adequately meets the level, give a middle mark. If it only just meets the level, give the lowest mark.

ex.t: Example: choosing a mark inside a level
b: Language level 4 to 6 means 'generally good'. A script with a good range and few errors: 6.
A script that meets the level adequately: 5.
A script that only just reaches the level: 4.

sections.h: Marking routines for the classroom: self, peer and teacher
p: You can use the mark scheme in the classroom, not only in exams. Self-marking: give students the key and a coloured pen. They mark their own work and write the reason for each lost mark. Peer marking: students swap papers and mark with the key, then explain disagreements. Teacher marking: you mark a sample (for example the writing task of six students) and give detailed comments.

Use a mix. Objective exercises (Exercise 2 matching, Exercise 4 multiple choice and all of Paper 2) can be self-marked quickly. Short-answer tasks (Exercises 1 and 3) are good for peer marking, because students learn from seeing alternatives that earn marks. Writing (Exercises 5 and 6) needs careful teacher marking at least every two weeks, and peer marking in between with a simple checklist.

ex.t: Example: a marking routine for a 40-minute lesson
b: 10 min: students do a reading exercise silently.
10 min: self-mark with the key, write reasons for lost marks.
10 min: pairs compare mistakes and find the evidence line in the text.
10 min: class discussion of the two hardest questions.

sections.h: Common marking mistakes teachers make
p: Marking by effort: giving marks because the student worked hard or the answer is long. Fix: only give marks for what the mark scheme rewards. Using half marks: Cambridge only awards whole marks, so do not use half marks in practice marking either. Penalising small spelling errors in short answers when the meaning is clear: Cambridge only judges spelling and grammar where the question tests them, and the meaning must be unambiguous. Fix: accept the answer if the meaning is clear.

Accepting 'almost right' answers: a near-miss that leaves out the tested idea gets no mark. Marking with grade thresholds in mind: marks come only from the mark scheme. Being influenced by handwriting or by your knowledge of the student: mark the script, not the student. Fix: cover names when you can, mark one question at a time across a class, and re-mark a few scripts after a break to check your own consistency.

b: A teacher gives 4.5 out of 6 for Content: wrong, only whole marks.
A teacher takes a mark away for 'fantasie' instead of 'fantasy' when meaning is clear: Cambridge would still give the mark in a short-answer question.
A teacher gives the top Content mark because the student wrote a lot: wrong, use the descriptors.

sections.h: Mark scheme vocabulary: a mini glossary
p: Candidate: the student taking the exam. Component or paper: one part of the exam (for example Paper 1). Exercise: one task inside a paper. Key: the list of correct answers. Descriptor or level descriptor: the statement that describes work at a level. Best fit: choosing the level that matches the work most closely. Whole marks: marks with no fractions. Credit: to give a mark. Creditable: worth a mark. Impede: to make communication difficult.

Moderation: checking marks to make sure they match the standard. Standardisation: practice marking and discussion so that all markers agree on the standard. Rubric: the instructions and information in a task (purpose, reader, format, prompts). Stimulus: the text or picture that starts a writing task. Prompt: a bullet or instruction students must answer.

ex.t: Example: use the words in a sentence
b: 'The student attempted a complex structure but errors did not impede understanding.'
'I will standardise with my colleagues before we mark the mocks.'
'The rubric tells you the purpose and the reader.'

units.activity: Print the first page of the June 2024 mark scheme for Paper 1 (0510/11). Highlight the six generic principles in six colours. Then write one sentence for each principle that tells a new colleague what it means in a classroom marking session.

check.q: What does a mark scheme tell you?
o: How examiners were told to give marks
How long to teach each topic

check.q: A key says: 'Award one mark for each detail up to a maximum of three marks.' A student gives four correct details. What is the mark?
Which statement matches positive marking?
o: Every spelling mistake loses a mark
Marks are not taken away for errors or omissions

units.title: Marking Paper 3 Speaking: Running, Recording and Marking the Test
units.summary: Learn how to run the Speaking test, apply the four marking criteria, choose the right mark inside a level, and keep the records Cambridge needs.

sections.h: Before the test: preparation and materials
p: Cambridge supplies Speaking Assessment cards with Teacher's/Examiner's Notes. The notes contain instructions, assessment criteria and the questions for each card. The teacher/examiner chooses one card for each candidate from the range provided. Candidates only receive a card for Part 2; the questions for Part 1 and Part 3 are in your notes and are not handed to students. Check the timetable for the Speaking test date window and expect to receive materials before it. Read the Cambridge Handbook for administration details.

Prepare a quiet room, a good recording device (test it first), the Speaking Examination Summary Form, a clock, and the cards. The test is in English and must be recorded in full for every student. Dictionaries are not allowed. Make sure each candidate knows the procedure and that you have enough time: about 10 to 15 minutes per candidate.

b: Recording equipment tested; spare batteries and a backup device.
Room quiet; a 'Do not disturb' sign on the door.
Cards, notes and the Summary Form ready.
Candidate list and an order of testing with times.

sections.h: Running the test: part by part
p: Introduction (about 1 minute, not assessed): start the recording, say your name, the candidate's number and name, and the date, welcome the candidate and read the examiner script. Warm-up (1 to 2 minutes, not assessed): a short friendly conversation using the questions provided, to help the candidate relax. Part 1 Interview (2 to 3 minutes, assessed): read out the topic from the script and ask the questions provided. Part 2 Short talk (3 to 4 minutes including 1 minute preparation, assessed): read the examiner script, give the card, allow up to one minute with no written notes, then the candidate talks on their own. The candidate can keep the card until the end of the talk. Part 3 Discussion (3 to 4 minutes, assessed): read the examiner script and ask the questions related to the Part 2 topic.

Stay on script. Use the questions provided. Ask follow-up prompts only as allowed in the notes. Let the candidate talk; do not finish their sentences or give them words, because that reduces the evidence of their own ability. The total test, from the start of the introduction to the end of Part 3, should be 10 to 15 minutes and must be recorded in full.

b: Talking more than the candidate.
Correcting mistakes during the test.
Giving hints that change the task.
Stopping the recording before Part 3 ends.

sections.h: The four marking criteria and what each level looks like
p: Speaking is marked out of 40: Grammar (10), Vocabulary (10), Development (10) and Pronunciation (10). Level 5 (9 to 10 marks). Grammar: a range of simple and complex structures, mostly accurate, errors rare and do not impede understanding. Vocabulary: a wide range, used precisely. Development: responses relevant and consistently well developed, communication maintained with ease. Pronunciation: clear, with intonation frequently used effectively to convey meaning.

Level 4 (7 to 8 marks). Grammar: a range of simple structures, with attempts at complex ones; errors often occur when attempting complex structures but do not impede understanding. Vocabulary: a sufficient range used appropriately. Development: relevant and mostly developed, with occasional support. Pronunciation: mostly clear, inaccuracies do not impede communication, intonation sometimes effective. Level 3 (5 to 6 marks). Grammar: simple structures, complex ones occasionally attempted, errors may impede understanding. Vocabulary: used mostly appropriately for simple ideas. Development: relevant with attempts at development, frequent support needed. Pronunciation: mostly clear, inaccuracies occasionally impede communication, intonation rarely effective.

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks). A limited range of only simple structures, errors frequently impede understanding; limited vocabulary for basic facts and opinions; responses mostly relevant but limited, communication may not always be maintained even with frequent support; pronunciation frequently unclear, intonation not effective. Level 1 (1 to 2 marks). Responses limited to widely spaced single words or short phrases; insufficient vocabulary for basic facts; responses brief and infrequent, communication not achieved even with frequent support; unclear pronunciation. 0 marks: no creditable response.

ex.t: Example: how the marks add up
b: Grammar 7 + Vocabulary 7 + Development 6 + Pronunciation 8 = 28 out of 40.
Mark each criterion separately, then add the four marks.
Use only whole marks.

sections.h: Choosing the exact mark: best fit and the three rules
p: Listen to the whole recording, then decide which level statement is the best fit for each criterion. Real performances rarely match one level exactly, so you may choose between two levels. When you have chosen a level, choose the mark inside it. If the work convincingly meets the level statement, give the highest mark. If it adequately meets the level statement, give the most appropriate mark in the middle of the range. If it just meets the level statement, give the lowest mark.

Marking should be positive: reward what the candidate can do, but clearly differentiate across the whole range of marks. Do not mark with grade thresholds in mind. Do not let one criterion influence another: a candidate with excellent vocabulary may still have weak pronunciation. Mark each criterion on its own evidence.

ex.t: Example: Level 4 Development, three mark options
b: 8 marks: responses relevant and mostly developed, communication maintained with only occasional support, throughout.
7 marks: just meets Level 4, a few unsupported answers but needs support more than occasionally.
If you cannot decide, listen again to Part 2 and Part 3 and count how often you had to prompt.

sections.h: Marking a sample short talk (teaching example)
p: Here is a short transcript of a candidate's Part 2 talk (written for this course): 'My topic is a hobby. My hobby is drawing. I draw every weekend, because it makes me feel calm. First, I choose a picture from a magazine and I try to copy it. Also, I sometimes draw my friends. They like it. I want to be better so I watch videos on the internet. In the future I would like to study art, if I get good marks.' (The candidate speaks clearly but pauses often, with a flat intonation.)

Suggested marks (for training). Grammar 6: simple structures mostly accurate and one complex structure (a conditional) attempted. Vocabulary 5: appropriate for simple ideas, little less common vocabulary. Development 5: relevant and with attempts at development (reasons given), but answers are short and the talk ends early. Pronunciation 6: mostly clear, intonation rarely effective. Total 22 out of 40. In your department, play a recording of a real candidate and compare marks without discussing first. Then talk about every difference of more than two marks.

b: Good: clear pronunciation and relevant answer.
Improve: add examples and comparisons; use phrases like 'for instance' and 'while'.
Practise: give a three-minute talk at home and record it.

sections.h: Records, recording quality and moderation
p: Record the marks for each candidate on the Speaking Examination Summary Form, which you download each year from the Cambridge samples database (www.cambridgeinternational.org/samples). Choose your country and enter 0510 to find the instructions, dates, methods of submission and forms for Paper 3. The marks on the form must be identical to the marks you submit to Cambridge.

If more than one teacher in your centre marks Speaking, you must carry out internal moderation so that all candidates are assessed to the same standard. Record the internally moderated marks on the form and submit them according to the Cambridge Handbook. Cambridge then externally moderates: you send the marks of all candidates and a sample of recordings, which should ideally include examples of each teacher's marking. Moderators write a short report with feedback on your marking and administration. Keep good quality recordings, label each file clearly and store them safely.

b: Name each file with centre number, candidate number and name.
Listen to the first 30 seconds of each recording to confirm it works.
Check that every mark on the form matches your records.
Keep a backup copy until results are released.

units.activity: With a colleague, role-play a 10-minute Speaking test with one Speaking Assessment card (use any topic card, such as 'a hobby you enjoy'). One of you is the examiner and one is the candidate. Record it. Then both mark the recording separately using the four criteria. Compare marks. For every criterion where you differ by two or more marks, find the exact words in the descriptor that support each mark.

check.q: How many marks are available for each Speaking criterion?
In the Speaking test, which parts are NOT assessed?
The candidate's work convincingly meets a level statement. Which mark do you give?
o: The highest mark in that level
The lowest mark in that level
The mark from the previous level

check.q: Where must you record the Speaking marks for each candidate?
o: On the Speaking Examination Summary Form
In an email to the parents

units.title: Marking Exercise 1 and Exercise 3: Short Answers and Notes
units.summary: Use the June 2024 cosplay blog and the car-free cities article to practise marking short answers and note-making.

sections.h: Exercise 1: the cosplay blog (8 marks)
p: In June 2024 Exercise 1 was a blog by a teenager called Lana about her hobby, cosplay. Cosplay means dressing up as a character from a film, book or video game. There are five one-mark questions and one three-mark question. Students write a word or a short phrase.

Look at the answers. Question 1 asks when the word cosplay was invented. The blog says the activity began in 1939 but the name was created in 1984, so the answer is (19)84. A student who writes 1939 is answering a different question. Question 2 asks what type of cosplay Lana prefers. She says she likes science fiction but she would choose fantasy before anything else, so the answer is fantasy.

b: Q1 When was the term invented? (19)84.
Q2 What type of cosplay does Lana prefer? fantasy.
Q3 Most famous cosplay contest? World Cosplay Summit.
Q4 What is she planning to be next? non-human role or character.
Q5 How would she like to make money? taking, selling or charging for photographs.
Q6 Three benefits (1 mark each, up to 3): many friends; gained confidence; more creative; learned to sew.

sections.h: What goes wrong in Exercise 1
p: Many wrong answers come from reading too fast. In Question 1, 1939 and 1984 are both in the text. In Question 2, science fiction and fantasy are both in the text. The student has found a real fact, but not the right one. Teach students to underline the question word (when, what type, how) and to match the answer to it.

In Question 6, a student may write 'she has made friends and gained confidence and become more creative and learned to sew and she is proud'. Only three marks are available, so do not count past three. Teach students to write the three clearest details and then stop.

b: Q1 'it started in 1939': 0 marks. The name was created in 1984.
Q2 'science fiction': 0 marks. She likes it but prefers fantasy.
Q5 'selling costumes': 0 marks. She says she cannot imagine selling hers.
Q6 'more friends, confidence, creative': 3 marks.

sections.h: Exercise 3: the car-free cities notes (7 marks)
p: Exercise 3 asks students to read a 400 to 500 word article and fill in short notes under headings. In June 2024 the article was 'Car-free cities'. The task: imagine you are giving a talk to classmates about reducing car use in cities. Question 8 asks for four policies that have been introduced. Question 9 asks for three things the writer tried to reduce his own car use.

The key for Question 8 lists five acceptable answers: removing parking places, car-free zones, charging drivers to enter parts of a city, better public transport, and parking charges outside the workplace. Any four earn the four marks. The key for Question 9 lists renting an e-bike or bike, sharing a car, making a personal travel plan or getting personalised advice, and downloading an app. Any three earn three marks.

b: Use words from the article. You do not have to use full sentences.
Keep each note short: a few words is enough.
Match the heading. Policies in Question 8, the writer's own actions in Question 9.
Do not repeat the same idea twice. 'Car-free zones' and 'zones without cars' count as one answer.

sections.h: Marking practice: is the answer in the right place?
p: In Exercise 3 an answer must belong under the right heading. For example, 'renting an e-bike' is something the writer tried himself, so it belongs in Question 9. If a student writes it as a policy in Question 8, it does not earn a mark there.

Another trap is copying too much. If a student copies a whole sentence that includes the correct idea together with wrong information, the answer can lose the mark, because it is no longer clear and accurate. Teach students to cut the answer down to the key words.

b: Q8 'removing parking places': 1 mark.
Q8 'renting an e-bike': 0 marks. This is the writer's own action, not a policy.
Q9 'sharing a car': 1 mark.
Q9 'London reduced traffic by 33 per cent': 0 marks. It is a result, not what the writer tried.

sections.h: Teaching Exercise 1 and Exercise 3: a 60-minute lesson plan
p: Aim: students find facts and make short notes accurately. Warm-up (5 minutes): show a headline and ask what the text will be about. Teach (10 minutes): show the question words and the type of answer each needs (when: a date or time; what type: a category; how: a method). Practise (15 minutes): students read a short text and answer five one-word questions. Mark together and discuss why wrong answers were wrong.

Then move to notes (20 minutes). Give a three-paragraph article and a notes frame with headings. Model one example on the board. Students complete the rest in pairs. Stop and check: is each note under the right heading? Is it short? Is it from the text? Finish (10 minutes) with a reflection: students write one rule they will follow next time.

ex.t: Example: question-word table to give students
b: When? date, time, year.
Who? name or job.
Where? place.
What type of ...? a category (fantasy, historical).
How? a method or way.
Why? a reason.

sections.h: More marking practice: Exercise 1 student answers
p: Use the June 2024 cosplay questions and these invented student answers to practise. Student A: Q1 '1984', Q2 'fantasy', Q3 'World Cosplay Summit', Q4 'non-human', Q5 'taking pictures at events and charging', Q6 'she made friends, she has more confidence, she learned to sew'. Marks: Q1 1, Q2 1, Q3 1, Q4 1 (non-human role or character), Q5 1 (taking and charging for photographs), Q6 3. Total 8 out of 8.

Student B: Q1 '1939', Q2 'science fiction', Q3 'EuroCosplay', Q4 'old man', Q5 'selling costumes', Q6 'she likes it'. Marks: Q1 0, Q2 0, Q3 0 (EuroCosplay is not the best-known contest), Q4 0 (the old man was a past character), Q5 0, Q6 0 (not one of the three listed details). Total 0 out of 8. Look at the pattern: Student B found real facts but answered the wrong question each time. The fix is to underline the question word and check the answer against it.

ex.t: Example: feedback you could write to Student B
b: Read each question word first: 'When was the name invented?' asks for the year of the name.
Check the type of answer: 'What type of cosplay does she prefer?' needs her top choice.
Practise with five more questions this week and bring your answers to me.

sections.h: Common difficulties in Exercises 1 and 3 and how to fix them
p: Writing a whole sentence and including a wrong detail: teach students to write only a few words. Giving the first thing they find: teach them to read the sentences before and after. Missing the plural or number in 'give three details': tell them to number their answers 1, 2, 3. Putting a correct fact under the wrong heading in notes: teach students to read the heading again before they write. Leaving blanks: remind them that every answer is a chance to score, and a guess is better than nothing.

Also watch for vocabulary problems: a student may find the right part of the text but not understand a key word such as 'policy' or 'initiative'. Teach them to guess meaning from the words around it and to build a personal word list from past papers. Over a term, students who do this build the topic vocabulary they need (environment, technology, health, travel and so on).

b: Give a short paragraph and five questions.
Students underline the question word, then underline the answer in the text.
They write the answer in no more than four words.
Check with a partner and swap.

units.activity: Take Exercise 1 and Exercise 3 from the June 2024 Paper 1 question paper in the download pack. Write the questions on a sheet and ask a colleague (or a student) to answer them. Then mark their answers using the mark scheme and write one feedback sentence for every lost mark.

check.q: Question 1 asks when the word 'cosplay' was invented. Which answer earns the mark?
The key for Question 8 gives five policies but the question has four marks. How many marks can a student score?
A student writes 'renting an e-bike' as a policy in Question 8. What is the mark?
o: 0, because it is the writer's own action, not a policy

units.title: Marking Exercise 2 and Exercise 4: Matching and Multiple Choice
units.summary: Practise matching statements to people (wild swimming) and multiple-choice reading (ToddlerLab) and learn to teach evidence-based answers.

sections.h: Exercise 2: wild swimming (9 marks)
p: Exercise 2 is a matching task. In June 2024 students read an article with four people, A Conor, B Emine, C Omar and D Ana, who enjoy wild swimming. Wild swimming means swimming outdoors in rivers, lakes and the sea. There were nine statements, 7(a) to 7(i). Students write the letter of the person each statement matches. Each is worth one mark.
The key is: (a) C, (b) B, (c) A, (d) D, (e) A, (f) D, (g) C, (h) B, (i) D. Notice that A, B, C and D are each used more than once. This is why students must find the idea, not just a matching word.

ex.t: Example: why each answer is right
b: (a) Better than a pool: Omar prefers fresh air to chemicals (C).
(b) Why they do not say where they swim: Emine says regular swimmers value private places (B).
(c) Prefers to go alone: Conor enjoys the times he has only himself for company (A).
(d) Surprised by wildlife: Ana saw a seal next to her and did not expect it (D).

sections.h: More Exercise 2 answers: the hard ones
p: (e) 'describes the effect on their state of mind' is A: Conor says he comes out feeling more positive than when he went in. (f) 'will go whatever the weather' is D: Ana says it does not matter how cold or wet it is. (g) 'a memory might have been inaccurate' is C: Omar says he had to be reminded of a worry he forgot, so his memory was incomplete.

(h) 'gives advice for newcomers' is B: Emine says to get into the water slowly and warm up quickly afterwards. (i) 'done something risky' is D: Ana goes in alone even though she knows it is not a good idea. These statements test R2 and R4: students must see the meaning behind the words, not only the same words.

ex.t: Example: teaching tip, the evidence line
b: For every answer, students underline the exact words in the text that prove it.
Then they write the letter.
If two texts seem to fit, they ask: which one is the best match for the whole statement?
This habit stops lucky guessing.

sections.h: Exercise 4: ToddlerLab (6 marks)
p: Exercise 4 has a longer article (550 to 600 words) and six multiple-choice questions with options A, B or C. In June 2024 the article was about ToddlerLab, a research laboratory at the University of London where scientists study how young children's brains develop. Questions 10 to 15 test main ideas, details, attitudes and the meaning of a phrase.

The key is: Q10 B, Q11 C, Q12 C, Q13 B, Q14 A, Q15 B. Q10 asks why Serena is interesting: because she wears a special cap with wires. Q11 asks what the second paragraph says: why it has been harder to study young children's brains than babies' brains. Q12 asks why she wears gloves: so cameras can record her hand movements. Q13: she begins her house-building task by watching a short video.

b: Q14 is A: the house-building task shows how young children follow instructions (the article says three-year-olds struggle with complex commands).
Q15 is B: 'as she does so' refers to Serena running around the room, which means moving rapidly.
Reference words such as 'so', 'this' and 'it' point back to an earlier idea. Teach students to look back one sentence.

sections.h: Marking and teaching with multiple choice
p: Multiple-choice marking is easy: one correct letter, one mark. Your teaching work is harder. A wrong option is called a distractor. Distractors often use words from the text but give a different meaning. For example, in Question 10 option A says 'unusually clever'. The article says there is nothing special about Serena except the cap, so A is wrong.

After a practice test, do not only say 'the answer is B'. Ask students to show the line in the text that proves B and the line that proves why A and C are wrong. This is how students learn the skill, not just the answer.

b: Give back the paper without marks.
Students find the evidence for each answer in pairs.
Check together with the key.
Students write one 'next time I will...' sentence about their biggest mistake.

sections.h: Teaching Exercise 2 matching: a step-by-step method
p: Step 1: read the statements and underline the main idea of each, for example 'why they avoid saying where they swim'. Step 2: read the first text and ask which statements it matches. Note the letter beside the statement. Step 3: read the second text and do the same. Step 4: compare: if two texts seem to fit one statement, look for the stronger match. Step 5: check that every statement has a letter and that you did not rely on one matching word.

Teach students to look for ideas in different words (paraphrase). For example, 'I tend not to reveal them' and 'explains why they avoid saying where they swim' say the same thing in different words. Good practice: give pairs two columns, one with text sentences and one with paraphrases, and ask them to match. This is the same skill that Exercise 2 tests: R2 and R3.

b: Text: 'I'll happily swim in the sea whenever I have the chance.' Paraphrase: 'enjoys swimming outdoors at every opportunity.'
Text: 'the trick is to get into the water slowly.' Paraphrase: 'gives advice to beginners.'
Students write 10 matching pairs from any article, then swap with another pair.

sections.h: Teaching Exercise 4 multiple choice: reading carefully and testing options
p: For Exercise 4, teach this routine. First, read the title and skim the text to get the general idea. Second, read question 1, find the paragraph it refers to, and read it carefully. Third, say the answer in your own words before you look at the options. Fourth, test each option: Is it stated or implied? Does it change a detail? Is it only partly true? Fifth, write the letter and move on. Do not spend more than a minute on one question.

Teach students about distractors. A distractor may use words from the text, but it answers a different question, goes too far (always, never, only), or reverses the meaning. Question types include main idea (what is the paragraph mainly about?), detail (what did Serena do first?), attitude (how does the writer feel?), and reference words (what does 'as she does so' refer to?). Practise each type separately in short drills before you use a whole exercise.

b: Question: Why does Serena wear gloves? Option A uses 'fingers more visible' (similar words, wrong reason).
Option B uses 'protect equipment' (not mentioned).
Option C 'to record her movements' matches the reflective material and cameras.

sections.h: Reading skills drills you can use in 10 minutes
p: Skim drill: give a text and 30 seconds. Students write the topic and three main ideas. Scan drill: give a list of five facts to find (a date, a name, a number, a place, a cost) and a time limit. Inference drill: give two sentences and ask what the writer suggests but does not say (for example, 'She checked her watch three times' suggests she is impatient). Reference drill: underline pronouns (it, they, this, so) and draw an arrow to the noun or idea they replace.

Link drill: give a paragraph with the linking words removed and a box of words (because, however, as a result, for example). Students put them back. This builds R2: understanding connections between ideas. Do one drill each lesson, so that skills become automatic over time.

ex.t: Example: inference sentences for a drill
b: 'He put the letter in the drawer and never mentioned it again.' (He may want to forget or hide it.)
'The queue stretched around the corner.' (The place is very popular.)
'I'm sure they'll all agree that they've gained confidence.' (The writer is positive about the hobby.)

units.activity: Choose Exercise 2 from the June 2024 paper. Cover the key. For each statement (a) to (i), write the letter AND the exact words from the text that prove it. Then check against the key. Count how many of your evidence lines you could quote.

check.q: In the June 2024 wild swimming task, which person says they prefer swimming alone (statement c)?
What is a distractor in a multiple-choice question?
o: A wrong option that looks attractive

check.q: In ToddlerLab Question 12, why is Serena asked to wear gloves?
o: To make her fingers more visible
So the cameras can record her movements

units.title: Marking Exercise 5 and Exercise 6: Writing with the Mark Scheme
units.summary: Learn the Content and Language tables, mark a sample email step by step, and plan a good review.

sections.h: The two writing tasks of June 2024
p: Exercise 5 (Question 16, 15 marks) asked for an informal email to a friend. The situation: you have decided to help at a sports event in your town next month. The email had to describe the event, say why you decided to help and explain what you will be doing, in about 120 to 160 words. A picture of a woman in sports clothes holding a folder was given.

Exercise 6 (Question 17, 15 marks) asked for a review of a new magazine for teenagers, to be posted on the school website. Four speech bubbles gave ideas: it is quite expensive; I would prefer longer articles; there are some interesting topics; I love the photos. Students could use these ideas and should add ideas of their own. Both tasks are marked with the same two tables: Table A Content (up to 6) and Table B Language (up to 9).

ex.t: Example: what is the same and what is different
b: Same: 120 to 160 words, 6 marks for Content, 9 for Language.
Different: Exercise 5 is informal (to a friend). Exercise 6 is more formal (a review for a school website).
Teach students to read: purpose, reader, format, prompts.

sections.h: Table A: Content (6 marks)
p: Content has two parts: task fulfilment and development of ideas. At 5 to 6 marks, the task is fulfilled, the content is fully relevant throughout, the style is consistently right for the text type, there is an excellent sense of purpose and audience, and ideas are very well developed. At 3 to 4 marks, each of these is 'generally' true. At 1 to 2 marks, the task is only partly fulfilled, content is only partly relevant, style is inconsistent or wrong, and there is only a limited attempt to develop ideas. 0 means no creditable response.
In simple words: did the student do what the task asked, for the right reader, in the right style, and did they explain their ideas with details?

b: Did the student cover every bullet or prompt?
Is everything relevant to the task?
Is the style right for a friend (informal) or a website review (more formal)?
Are there details, reasons or examples, not just one line per bullet?

sections.h: Table B: Language (9 marks)
p: Language also has two parts: range and accuracy, and organisation. At 7 to 9 marks, content is communicated skilfully, with a wide range of common and less common vocabulary, a wide range of simple and complex structures, a high level of accuracy (occasional errors do not impede communication), effective organisation and a wide range of linking words.

At 4 to 6 marks, content is communicated clearly, with a range of common vocabulary and attempts at less common words, a range of simple structures and attempts at complex ones, a generally good level of accuracy and a range of linking words used generally appropriately. At 1 to 3 marks, content lacks clarity, only common vocabulary and simple structures are used, and errors impede communication, with a limited attempt at organisation and linking.

b: Vocabulary: only common words, or some less common words too?
Structures: only simple sentences, or some complex sentences (because, although, if)?
Accuracy: do errors stop you understanding?
Organisation: paragraphs, clear order, linking words such as also, because, however?

sections.h: Marking a sample email (teaching example)
p: Read this sample answer to Question 16 (written for this course, not a Cambridge script, about 130 words): 'Hi Sam, How are you? I have some good news to tell you. Next month there is a big running race in our town and I decided to help there as a volunteer. The race is for everyone, children and adults, and about 500 people will take part. It start at the town park at nine o'clock and finish near the market. I decided to help because I love sport and I want to do something good for my town. Also, my teacher said it will be a good experience for my CV. I will be giving water to the runners and I will help to show them the way. I will also say well done to them at the end. Would you like to come and help with me? It would be more fun together! Write soon, Tolu'.

Marking: Content. All three bullets are covered, ideas are developed with some detail, and the informal style is right. Content: 5 out of 6. Language. Content is communicated clearly, with simple structures used well and some complex ones (because, I decided to...). Errors such as 'It start' and 'finish' are small and do not impede meaning. Vocabulary is mostly common. Linking words (also, because) are used generally appropriately. Language: 5 out of 9. Total: about 10 out of 15. Different markers may differ by one mark; the important thing is to use the table to explain your decision.

ex.t: Example: how to lift this script
b: Add a wider range of vocabulary (for example, 'cheer them on', 'a great opportunity').
Use more complex structures (for example, 'If the weather is good, I will ...').
Check agreement: 'It starts ... and finishes ...'.
Add a little more detail to the reason for helping.

sections.h: Teaching Exercise 5 (informal email): plan, write, check
p: Lesson stages. Stage 1 (10 minutes): read the task and underline the purpose (to tell a friend), the reader (a friend), the format (email) and the three prompts. Stage 2 (10 minutes): plan: one short paragraph for each prompt, with one idea, one detail and one example. Stage 3 (20 minutes): write 120 to 160 words, using a friendly style: greeting, contractions (I'm, don't), friendly phrases (Guess what!, I can't wait), and a closing. Stage 4 (10 minutes): check for verb forms, word endings, spelling and linking words.

Teach a simple email frame: greeting; opening sentence (why you are writing); paragraph 1 (prompt 1 with detail); paragraph 2 (prompt 2 with reason); paragraph 3 (prompt 3 with what you will do); closing question or invitation; sign-off. Encourage students to use a few complex structures (although, if, because, who, which) and a few less common words. Mark a sample with the Content and Language tables and give two targets only.

ex.t: Example: friendly and formal openings and closings
b: Informal: 'Hi Sam, How are you? I've got some great news!' ... 'Write soon, Tolu.'
Formal: 'Dear Editor, I am writing to review ...' ... 'Yours faithfully, Tolu Bello.'
Teach students to choose the opening and closing that fit the reader.

sections.h: Teaching Exercise 6 (review, report, essay or article)
p: Exercise 6 asks for a more formal response, and the text type changes between series. For a review (as in June 2024) a good structure is: opening (what you are reviewing and a general opinion), main points with reasons and examples (what is good, what could be better), and a closing recommendation. Use the prompts and add ideas of your own. For a report: heading, introduction, findings in short paragraphs, and recommendations. For an article: an interesting opening, clear paragraphs and a final thought. For an essay: introduction, main body with reasons and examples, conclusion.

Teach register: semi-formal language, fewer contractions, full sentences, and polite phrases such as 'I would recommend' and 'It would be better if'. Use the speech bubbles or prompts but add at least one idea of the student's own. Remember: a review needs opinion words and evaluation, not only description.

b: Opening: 'The new magazine for teenagers is well designed, although it has some weaknesses.'
Positive: photos, interesting topics, with an example of each.
Negative: price and short articles, with a reason.
Closing: 'Overall, I would recommend it to friends, especially if the price comes down.'

sections.h: A second marking example: a formal review (teaching example)
p: Read this sample answer to Question 17, written for this course (about 140 words, not a Cambridge script): 'The new teen magazine, called Today, is quite good but not perfect. First, the photos are beautiful and they makes the pages look attractive. Also, there are interesting topics such as music, school life and new technology. I especially liked the article about young inventors. However, the magazine is expensive, so many students may not buy it every month. Moreover, some articles are very short, and I would prefer longer articles because I like to learn more details. In my opinion, the writer should add a page for readers' letters. Overall, I recommend this magazine to anyone who enjoys reading about teenage life, but the price should be lower.'

Marking. Content: the task is fulfilled, content is relevant, a review style is used, and ideas are developed with reasons and an example (the article about inventors) and a suggestion of the student's own (readers' letters). Content: 5 out of 6. Language: a range of simple and some complex structures (because, so, although-type contrasts), good linking words (First, Also, However, Moreover, Overall), a few errors ('they makes') that do not impede meaning, a mostly common vocabulary with a few less common items. Language: 6 out of 9. Total: about 11 out of 15.

b: Check subject-verb agreement (they make, not they makes).
Use more precise vocabulary (for example 'eye-catching', 'informative', 'good value').
Add one more complex sentence, such as 'Although the photos are excellent, I think the text could be more detailed.'

units.activity: Write your own 120 to 160 word answer to the June 2024 magazine review (Question 17) using at least two of the speech-bubble ideas and one idea of your own. Then mark it with Tables A and B: write the Content mark, the Language mark, and one sentence of evidence for each.
