Which Language band says 'content is communicated clearly' with a 'generally good' level of accuracy?
What should you do first when marking a writing script?
o: Read the whole script and decide which level fits best
Give the top mark in the level

units.title: Paper 2 Listening, Past Papers and the Examiner's Report
units.summary: Learn how to use the June 2024 Listening paper and mark scheme, how to run a past-paper lesson, and how to use an examiner's report to improve your teaching.

sections.h: Paper 2 Listening: the shape of the paper
p: Paper 2 has 40 multiple-choice questions in five exercises and takes about 50 minutes, including 6 minutes to copy answers onto a separate answer sheet. Every recording is played twice. The June 2024 paper (0510/21) has audio, a mark scheme and a transcript.

Exercise 1 (Q1 to Q8): eight short extracts with four picture options A to D. Exercise 2 (Q9 to Q18): five short extracts, two questions each, with three options. Exercise 3 (Q19 to Q26): one talk, complete eight sentences with three options. Exercise 4 (Q27 to Q32): six short monologues, match each to one of eight statements (A to H). Exercise 5 (Q33 to Q40): an interview, eight questions with three options.

b: Exercise 1: 8 marks. Exercise 2: 10 marks. Exercise 3: 8 marks. Exercise 4: 6 marks. Exercise 5: 8 marks.
Total: 40 marks.
Where to check the audio: Cambridge Handbook, www.cambridgeinternational.org/eoguide.

sections.h: The June 2024 Listening answer key
p: Questions 1 to 8: A, C, C, B, D, C, D, A. Questions 9 to 18: C, B, B, C, A, A, C, B, A, B. Questions 19 to 26: C, A, B, A, C, B, A, C.

Questions 27 to 32 (matching): G, A, F, B, C, H. Questions 33 to 40: C, B, B, A, C, A, C, B. Each correct answer earns one mark and there are no half marks. Keep a copy of the transcript beside the key so you can show students the exact words that prove each answer.

ex.t: Example: mark and analyse in 20 minutes
b: Give each student the answer key to self-mark in a different colour pen.
Make a table of the five exercises and ask students to count marks per exercise.
Find the exercise with the lowest total across the class: that is the next lesson.
Replay one extract with the transcript and underline the key words.

sections.h: Running a past-paper lesson
p: A good past-paper lesson has four steps. Step 1, predict: before listening or reading, students look at the questions and guess the type of answer needed (a name, a number, a feeling). Step 2, do it under test conditions with the real timing. Step 3, mark with the mark scheme. Step 4, learn: talk about why wrong answers were wrong.

Do not use every past paper as a test. Use some as practice for one skill only. For example, use only Exercise 3 of Paper 2 for a short 10-minute listening practice at the start of a lesson. This gives students many chances to practise without tiring them.

ex.t: Example: one week plan with past papers
b: Monday: Paper 1 Exercise 2 (matching), 20 minutes, mark together.
Wednesday: Paper 2 Exercise 4 (monologues), play twice, then discuss clues.
Friday: Paper 1 Exercise 5 (email), write in 25 minutes, peer-mark with Table A and Table B.

sections.h: Using the examiner's report
p: The Principal Examiner's Report for Teachers is published for each exam series on the Cambridge website. It tells you how students answered each question, what the best answers did, what went wrong, and what to teach next. Read it with the question paper and the mark scheme open. For each question ask: what was the common mistake, and what could I do in my next lesson to avoid it?

Use the report to plan, not just to read. Make a one-page action list: three things students did well, three things to change in your teaching, and the exercise you will practise first next term. Share the page with your department.

ex.t: Example: turning a report into action
b: Report says: students copy long sentences in short-answer questions. Action: teach 'cut to the key words' in two lessons.
Report says: students match words, not ideas. Action: do the 'evidence line' routine.
Report says: writing is too short. Action: practise adding reasons and examples.

sections.h: Your resource pack for Week 2
p: In the download pack for this course you will find: the June 2024 Paper 1 question paper and mark scheme, the June 2024 Paper 2 mark scheme, and the Paper 2 audio (MP3). Cambridge also publishes the Paper 2 question paper, the transcript and the examiner's report on its website for teachers.

Always check that you have the paper for the right year and the right paper number (0510/11 for Reading and Writing, 0510/21 for Listening). Keep your own copy of each mark scheme and write notes on it after each lesson.

b: Question paper 0510/11 June 2024.
Mark scheme 0510/11 June 2024.
Mark scheme 0510/21 June 2024.
Audio for Paper 2 (MP3) and the transcript from Cambridge.

sections.h: Teaching each Listening exercise
p: Exercise 1 (eight short extracts with picture options): train students to notice the differences among the four pictures before the recording, then to listen for the detail that matches (a time, an object, a place). Exercise 2 (five extracts, two questions each): teach students to read both questions first and listen for opinions, reasons and implied meaning. Exercise 3 (one talk, eight sentence completions): the sentences follow the order of the talk, so students should keep their place; options are words or short phrases.

Exercise 4 (six short monologues, eight statements): each speaker matches one statement, and two are unused. Teach students to listen for the main idea of each speaker, not single words, and to cross out used statements. Exercise 5 (an interview, eight multiple-choice questions): the questions follow the interview in order. Teach students to listen for the main speaker's opinions and reasons, and for words that signal change such as 'but' or 'although'.

b: Predict (3 minutes): look at the questions and guess the topic and answer type.
Listen (5 minutes): play twice.
Check (4 minutes): self-mark with the key.
Transcript (3 minutes): find the exact words for two answers and one mistake.

sections.h: Practical tips for setting up listening practice
p: Check your audio file and speakers before the lesson. Sit students so that all can hear equally well. Play the recording from beginning to end without stopping during a test-style practice. For learning practice (not a test) you may pause and replay a short extract to teach a point. Use the transcript to teach: ask students to listen again while reading it and mark the words that gave the answer.

For the real exam, your exams officer and the Cambridge Handbook tell you how and when to access the audio, how to prepare the room and equipment, and how to check the audio in advance. Always read the Handbook for the year of the exam.

ex.t: Example: a checklist before playing audio
b: Is the file the right exercise?
Is the volume clear at the back of the room?
Do students have the question paper and the answer sheet?
Is the room quiet and are phones off?

sections.h: Turning the examiner's report into a department plan
p: Make this a team habit. Step 1: before the meeting, each teacher reads the report for one paper and prepares notes. Step 2: in the meeting, share the three biggest strengths and three biggest weaknesses for that paper. Step 3: link each weakness to an assessment objective (for example R4 or W4). Step 4: decide teaching changes, such as new lessons, new practice tasks or new marking routines. Step 5: set a date to check progress with a mock exam.

Keep a one-page summary for each series. After three or four years, you will see patterns and know which skills need constant attention. Keep the reports with the question papers and mark schemes in a shared folder so that new teachers can learn quickly.

b: Paper and series.
Three strengths in students' answers.
Three weaknesses and their assessment objectives.
Teaching actions, who will do them and when.

units.activity: Create a one-page Past Paper Plan for the next four weeks. For each week write: the paper and exercise, the skill being practised (R1 to R4, W1 to W4, L1 to L4), how you will mark it, and one feedback action. Then read the June 2024 examiner's report for Paper 1 and add two actions that come from it.

check.q: How many times is each recording played in Paper 2 Listening?
In the June 2024 Listening mark scheme, what is the answer to Question 27?
What is the best way to use the examiner's report?
o: Read it once and forget it
Use it only to find grade boundaries
Give it to students without discussion
Make an action list for your next lessons

units.title: Standardising Marking, Giving Feedback and Improving Results
units.summary: Run a standardisation meeting, give feedback that moves students forward, and use a marking portfolio to prove and improve your expertise.

sections.h: Running a department standardisation meeting
p: Standardisation means that all markers apply the same standard. It is required for internal moderation of Speaking and it improves consistency in writing too. Prepare four to six scripts or recordings from different levels. Ask each teacher to mark them alone with the mark scheme and write the marks and a reason for each. In the meeting, show all marks on a board and look for scripts where marks differ by more than one or two. Discuss those first, using the descriptors, and agree on the best-fit level and mark.

Agree a set of 'reference scripts' that the whole department keeps as examples at each level. Write short notes about why each reference script earned its marks. Repeat the exercise at the start of each marking period. For Speaking, listen to recordings together. Keep minutes with the agreed standard so new teachers can learn it.

b: 5 min: purpose and rules (descriptors first, opinions second).
15 min: individual marking of two scripts.
15 min: compare, discuss differences, agree marks.
10 min: file the agreed scripts and plan the next meeting.

sections.h: Feedback that moves students forward
p: Good feedback is specific, kind and useful. Give two or three targets, not twenty. Link each target to a skill code and a clear action. For writing, use the Content and Language tables: 'Content 4/6: you answered all three prompts, but add a reason and an example to each (W1). Language 5/9: use two linking words in each paragraph and check word endings (W2, W3).' For reading and listening, show where in the text the evidence was and what question word to look for.

Use methods like 'two stars and a wish', comment banks that you reuse, coded marking (for example SP for spelling, T for tense, WW for wrong word, ^ for missing word) and short one-to-one conferences. Always ask students to act: rewrite one paragraph, redo the corrected questions, or practise one pronunciation point. A mark without action does not improve learning.

ex.t: Example: a comment bank (reuse and adapt)
b: Add a reason: 'Because ...' or 'This is important because ...'.
Add an example: 'For example ...'.
Link your ideas: use however, therefore, in addition.
Check verb forms: look at each past tense verb again.

sections.h: Planning support after the mock exams
p: After marking mocks, sort students into three groups: on track, close to the next grade, and needing urgent support. For each group plan an action. On track: extension tasks with more challenging texts and Level 5 speaking practice. Close to the next grade: small-group lessons on the one or two exercises with the lowest marks. Needing urgent support: one-to-one or small-group work on basics (key vocabulary, simple sentence accuracy, listening for specific information) and short daily practice.

Set a review date, usually four weeks later. Re-check with a short test of the target exercise. Share progress with the student and, where useful, the parent. Remember that Cambridge grade boundaries are set after the exam, so do not tell students they 'will get' a grade; tell them what they can do now and what they need to do next.

ex.t: Example: a four-week support plan for one student
b: Week 1: reading Exercise 3 notes, two practice tasks and feedback.
Week 2: listening Exercise 2, two practice tasks with transcript.
Week 3: writing a formal review with a plan and a model, then rewrite.
Week 4: short test of the same three skills and a new target.

sections.h: Your marking portfolio: show that you can mark like Cambridge
p: Build a marking portfolio. It helps you grow as a Cambridge educator and is useful evidence for your school and for future roles such as examiner or moderator. Include: a marked set of Exercise 1 and Exercise 3 answers with reasons for each mark; a marked matching and multiple-choice exercise with the evidence lines from the text; two writing scripts marked with Tables A and B with comments; a Listening paper analysed by exercise; and one Speaking recording marked with the four criteria, with notes on the exact descriptor words.

Add a one-page reflection: what you learned about marking, what you changed in your teaching, what is still difficult, and what you will do next. Keep the portfolio and update it each term. A teacher who can explain their marks with the descriptors, and who has an improvement plan from the results, shows real expertise.

b: Reading short answers marked and explained.
Matching and multiple choice with evidence lines.
Two writing scripts marked with Tables A and B and feedback.
One Listening paper analysed by exercise.
One Speaking recording marked with four criteria.
One-page reflection.

units.activity: Complete your marking portfolio from the checklist above. Use real June 2024 materials from this course for the reading and listening tasks, and your own students' (or colleagues') work for writing and speaking. Bring it to your first standardisation meeting and ask one colleague to review it.

check.q: What is the purpose of a standardisation meeting?
o: To make sure all markers apply the same standard
To avoid using the mark scheme

check.q: Which feedback is most useful?
o: Two or three specific targets linked to skills and actions
A long list of every error

check.q: After a mock exam, what should you do for students close to the next grade?
o: Teach small-group lessons on their weakest exercises
Tell them they will definitely get the grade

units.title: Welcome to Week 3: Long-Term Planning, the Academic Year Map
units.summary: Plan the whole course like a road trip: map the year, protect an exam buffer, weave the four skills together and set decision milestones.

sections.h: The road-trip idea
p: Think of teaching the Cambridge IGCSE ESL (0510) course as planning a long road trip. Long-term and medium-term planning is your road map. Prerequisite knowledge is checking that your car has fuel before you leave. Initial assessment is checking the dashboard to see whether any part needs fixing right now. This week you will build the map and check how ready your passengers are.

Planning is done at two levels. Long-term planning is the big picture: the whole one-year or two-year course on your school calendar. Medium-term planning is the monthly blocks: one theme over four to six weeks, with clear learning targets. A good plan saves time, stops you from forgetting a skill, and lets you tell students, parents and colleagues where the course is going.

Cambridge says a school curriculum should be broad, balanced and consistent, with smooth progression, and that the school must write its own schemes of work because the curriculum is built locally. The syllabus and papers are the same for everyone; the plan is yours.

ex.t: By the end of Week 3 you will be able to
b: Draw a year map with an exam buffer and thematic modules.
Write a medium-term scheme of work for a 4 to 6 week theme.
Say what students should already know before the course starts.
Build and use a diagnostic test with a simple scoring guide.
Update your KWL learning tracker.

sections.h: Step 1: Count your real time
p: Start with facts. Cambridge plans about 130 guided learning hours for an IGCSE subject. For English as a second language in the earlier Cambridge stages it suggests about 120 to 150 hours a year, or 4 to 5 hours a week. Guided learning hours means time when a teacher teaches or guides the students. Count how many ESL lessons you have each week, how long each lesson is, and how many weeks of real teaching you have after holidays, public days, school trips, tests and mock exams.

A school year is usually 36 to 40 weeks long, but many of those weeks are not full teaching weeks. If you teach three 45-minute lessons a week for 32 weeks, you have about 72 hours in a year, which is far below 130 hours over a two-year course unless you add more lessons, homework or clubs. Doing this sum in week one tells you whether your plan is realistic.

b: 3 lessons a week x 45 minutes = 2 hours 15 minutes a week.
32 teaching weeks x 2.25 hours = 72 hours in one year.
Two years = 144 hours. This meets the 130-hour guide, but with little spare time.
If you teach only one year before the exam, you must add lessons or independent work.

sections.h: Step 2: Protect the exam buffer
p: A standard school year is about 36 to 40 weeks. Plan new lessons for only 30 to 32 weeks. Leave the final 6 to 8 weeks of the course empty on your plan. Use that time for past-paper practice, time-management drills, speaking practice tests and revision. This is called the exam buffer. Without it, teachers often reach the exam still teaching new content, and students never practise under exam conditions.

The buffer also protects you from surprises: lost days, student absences, power cuts, a failed recording device before a Speaking test. When something goes wrong, you take time from the buffer, not from your students' last chance to practise.

b: Weeks 1 to 31: new teaching, one mock at about week 20.
Weeks 32 to 38: past papers, timed practice, targeted revision and the Speaking tests (check the Cambridge timetable for your window).
Never let new content push into the buffer. If you fall behind, shorten a module, do not remove the buffer.

sections.h: Step 3: Weave the four skills together
p: The exam tests Reading, Writing, Listening and Speaking. Your plan must keep all four skills moving all year. You cannot spend six months only on reading and then six months only on speaking, because skills fade without practice and students will not be ready for Paper 3. Use a weekly pattern, for example in a four-lesson week: one Reading lesson, one Writing lesson, one Listening lesson and one Speaking and language lesson. Put five minutes of vocabulary at the start of each lesson and one-minute reflection at the end.

The weightings help you plan. Reading is 35 per cent of the written grade, Writing 35 per cent and Listening 30 per cent. Speaking is separately graded from 1 to 5 but it is compulsory, so it needs regular practice. Add a few full past-paper exercises under timed conditions each month, and a mock at the end of each term.

b: Mon: Reading strategy and one exercise (skim, scan, careful reading).
Tue: Writing (plan, write, check).
Thu: Listening (predict, listen, check with transcript).
Fri: Speaking and language (pair talk, pronunciation, grammar or vocabulary).

sections.h: Step 4: Divide the year into thematic modules
p: Do not plan lesson by lesson at the start. Divide the calendar into thematic modules, each about 4 to 6 weeks, based on popular topics from the syllabus such as the environment, health, food, film, travel, technology, celebrations, science, the arts and shopping. For example: Module 1 Global Travel, Module 2 Technology and Society, Module 3 Health and Fitness.

A theme gives the language a home. Students learn vocabulary and grammar for the theme, read and listen to texts about it, write texts about it and speak about it. The same words come back in all four skills, which helps memory. Choose themes that are interesting to your students, and put the hardest themes after students have built confidence.

b: Year 1 Term 1: Travel and Celebrations.
Year 1 Term 2: Technology and Society, Shopping.
Year 1 Term 3: Health and Fitness, Food.
Year 2 Term 1: Environment, Film and the Arts.
Year 2 Term 2: Science, mixed review, mock exams.
Year 2 Term 3: exam buffer.

sections.h: Step 5: Set milestones and decision points
p: A milestone is a date when you stop and decide. Put these on your year map: the end of the diagnostic period, the end of each term (mock exam and review), the date you must tell the exams officer about entries and access arrangements, the Speaking test window, and the final practice papers. At each milestone ask: Are we on time? Which skill is weakest? Who needs extra help?

Some older versions of IGCSE ESL had a Core tier and an Extended tier. If you teach one of those versions, your plan needs a milestone to decide which students enter which tier. IMPORTANT: the 2024 to 2026 syllabus (Speaking Endorsement) that this course follows has no tiers. All candidates take the same Paper 1 and Paper 2. For this syllabus, the important milestones are about readiness, Speaking tests and entries. Always check the syllabus for your exam year and ask your exams officer.

ex.t: Example: milestones on a year map
b: Week 3: diagnostic results and learner profiles.
Week 12 and 24: term mock and review.
Week 28: entries and access arrangements submitted (check your real dates).
Week 32: start of buffer weeks.
Speaking test: dates set with the exams officer using the Cambridge timetable.

sections.h: Factors that affect your plan
p: Cambridge lists factors that shape timetabling. Inside the school: the organisation, resources such as staff and rooms, compulsory subjects or choice, the English level of learners, multi-levelling or fixed year groups, co-curricular activities and employment contracts. Outside the school: Cambridge programme and qualification requirements, recommended hours, national requirements, ministry rules and university entry rules.

Ask yourself: How long is each lesson? Do I have a room with good sound for Listening and a quiet space for Speaking tests? Do I have recording equipment? Are my classes mixed in level? A long lesson gives time for several different activities, but only if you prepare enough. A short lesson often becomes teacher talk, so plan quick pair tasks.

b: Take a sheet of paper and draw 38 boxes for the weeks.
Cross out holidays and known events.
Mark the buffer (the last 6 to 8 weeks).
Write your themes and the milestones.
Show it to a colleague and ask: 'Is this realistic?'

units.activity: Create a one-page Year Map for your class: weeks, holidays, thematic modules, the 6 to 8 week exam buffer, term mocks and decision milestones. Write the number of guided learning hours you really have. Share it with your head of department.

check.q: How many weeks should you plan for new lessons in a 36 to 40 week year?
What is the exam buffer used for?
o: Past papers, timing practice and revision

check.q: Why should the plan weave all four skills together all year?
o: Skills fade without regular practice and all four are examined

units.title: Medium-Term Planning: Writing a Scheme of Work
units.summary: Zoom into one 4 to 6 week theme and fill in a four-column scheme of work with language focus, exam skill focus and an assessment goal.

sections.h: What is a scheme of work?
p: A scheme of work is the middle layer of planning. It zooms in on one theme, usually four to six weeks, and breaks the year goals into actions: what language you will teach, which exam skills you will practise, and how you will check learning. It sits between the year map and your daily lesson plans.

Cambridge provides example schemes of work and teacher guides on its School Support Hub for many subjects. Use them as a starting point, but adapt them to your students, because Cambridge says schools should make their own schemes so that the syllabus is locally relevant and well taught.

b: Long-term: the year map (about 36 to 40 weeks).
Medium-term: scheme of work for a 4 to 6 week theme.
Short-term: lesson plans (one lesson or one week).

sections.h: The four columns you must fill in
p: For every 4 to 6 week theme, fill in four things. First, Theme and timeline: the name of the module and which weeks it covers. Second, Language focus: the grammar and vocabulary you will teach. Third, Cambridge exam skill focus: which reading, writing, listening and speaking skills (and which exam exercises) you will practise. Fourth, Assessment goal: how you will check what students learned.

Here is one example from the plan you were given. Theme and timeline: Module 2, Sport and Health, Weeks 5 to 10. Language focus: modal verbs such as should and must, and adjectives for physical fitness. Exam skill focus: Reading, skimming short texts; Writing, writing a school magazine article. Assessment goal: a formative quiz on the layout and tone of an article.

b: Theme and timeline: ______ (weeks __ to __).
Language focus: grammar ______; vocabulary ______.
Cambridge exam skill focus: Reading ______; Writing ______; Listening ______; Speaking ______.
Assessment goal: ______ (what, when, how marked).

sections.h: A full four-week example: Module 2, Sport and Health
p: Week 1. Language: adjectives for health and fitness (fit, healthy, tired, energetic, strong). Reading: skim and scan a short article about school sports (Exercise 1 style questions). Listening: a short extract about a sports day (Exercise 1 style, picture options). Speaking: pair talk, 'What sport do you enjoy, and why?' Homework: write five sentences using the new adjectives.

Week 2. Language: modal verbs should, shouldn't, must, mustn't, have to for advice and rules. Reading: matching task, four people give opinions on exercise (Exercise 2 style). Writing: plan an informal email giving advice to a friend who wants to get fit (Exercise 5 style). Speaking: give advice using modal verbs. Week 3. Language: linking words for addition and contrast (also, however, although). Reading: notes from an article under headings (Exercise 3 style). Writing: write the first draft of a school magazine article, 120 to 160 words, with an introduction, two main points and a conclusion. Listening: an interview about healthy eating (Exercise 5 style).

Week 4. Language: review, correct common errors from the drafts. Writing: improve the article using feedback; peer review with a checklist. Speaking: a two-minute short talk on 'How to stay healthy', with one minute of preparation (Paper 3 Part 2 style). Assessment goal: formative quiz on article layout and tone (headline, introduction, paragraphs, a friendly but semi-formal style) and a short speaking check. Reflection: students record what they can now do and what is still hard.

ex.t: Checks that you built a good scheme
b: Does every week have all four skills?
Does the language focus appear in reading, writing and speaking tasks?
Does the module end with an assessment that matches the exam skill?
Is there time for feedback and a second attempt?

sections.h: Write clear learning targets
p: A learning target says what the student will be able to do, in simple words. Use 'I can' statements, such as: 'I can use should and must to give advice.' 'I can skim a text to find the main idea in two minutes.' 'I can write a magazine article with a clear introduction and conclusion.' Link each target to a skill code from the syllabus where possible, for example R1 or W2.

Targets help you plan, help students understand why they are doing a task, and give you something to measure at the end of the module. Share the targets with students at the start of each module and review them at the end.

b: R1: I can find specific facts in an article about health.
W2: I can link my ideas with also, however and because.
W4: I can write in the right style for a school magazine.
L2: I can understand what a speaker thinks about exercise.
S3: I can add a reason and an example to my speaking answers.

sections.h: Plan assessment inside the module
p: Assessment for learning means checking understanding during the module so you can adjust your teaching. Plan small checks: a quick quiz, an exit ticket, a short writing task marked with the Content and Language tables, a five-minute speaking check. Keep a record. At the end of the module, give one bigger task in the style of the exam, and use the mark scheme or level descriptors to mark it.

Cambridge examiners mark positively: they reward what the student can do. Your classroom marking should do the same. Give two or three clear targets, not twenty corrections. Then plan time in the next module to practise the targets.

ex.t: Example: assessment plan for one module
b: Week 2: exit ticket on modal verbs.
Week 3: peer check of an article draft with a checklist.
Week 4: article marked with Content and Language tables; short speaking check.
Next module: use the targets from this module as your starter activities.

sections.h: Review and improve your scheme
p: After each module, spend 15 minutes reviewing your scheme. What went well? What took too long? Which tasks did students like? Where did most students lose marks? Change the scheme for next time. Cambridge says that curriculum development is an ongoing process of gathering evidence and evaluating it, so every scheme is a draft that you improve each year.
Keep your schemes in one shared folder. If you work in a department, compare schemes and share the best ideas. A new teacher who joins your school can then see exactly how the course runs.

b: List what students learned (check against the targets).
List three problems.

units.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: The Starting Line
units.summary: Know what students must be able to do before Day 1 of the IGCSE ESL course, and how to bridge the gaps if they cannot yet.

sections.h: What is prerequisite knowledge?
p: Before a student can write a good 150-word formal piece for the exam, they must already know how to build a basic paragraph. Prerequisite knowledge is the foundation a student needs before Day 1. It is like fuel in the car. If the tank is empty, the best map cannot help.

Cambridge suggests that IGCSE students have already studied a course in English as a second language, such as Cambridge Lower Secondary or a national course at the same level. This is advice, not a rule. Some students will have a strong base; others will need extra help. Your job is to find out early and plan support.

b: The IGCSE course moves at a fast pace with about 130 hours of teaching.
Students with gaps in basics lose marks in Language (9 of the 15 marks in each writing task).
Finding gaps in week one saves months of struggle later.

sections.h: The four baseline skills for IGCSE ESL (0510)
p: 1. CEFR language level. Ideally students enter at a strong A2 to lower B1 level on the Common European Framework of Reference. At A2 a student can understand and use common phrases about familiar things, such as family, shopping and daily routines. At B1 a student can deal with most everyday situations, describe experiences and give simple reasons for opinions. The course will take them towards B2, where they can express opinions with some fluency.

2. Basic reading comprehension. Students should be able to read a simple, 200-word factual text, such as a short news article, and answer straightforward Who, What, Where and When questions. 3. Sentence mechanics. They must know that a sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, and understand basic subject-verb agreement, for example why 'He play football' is wrong. 4. Listening and following directions. They must be able to follow spoken, multi-step instructions in English at a normal, clear speed, such as 'Open your books at page ten, read the second paragraph and underline the date.'

ex.t: Quick signs a student is below the starting line
b: Cannot find a simple fact in a short text.
Writes without capital letters or full stops.
Often says or writes 'he go', 'she have', 'they is'.
Needs every instruction repeated or translated.

sections.h: How to check each skill quickly
p: You do not need a long test for each baseline skill. Reading: give a 200-word factual text with five simple questions. Sentence mechanics: ask students to write five sentences about their weekend and check capitals, full stops and verb agreement. Listening: give three instructions in a row and see if they do the task. Level: a short conversation shows you whether they speak at A2 or B1 level. All of these fit into the diagnostic test in the next unit.
Look at patterns, not single mistakes. One student who forgets a capital letter is normal. A student who forgets them in every sentence needs a lesson on it.

b: Say: 'Write your name at the top, draw a line under it, and then write today's date on the right.'
Say it once at normal speed.
Watch who completes all three steps.
Note students who complete only one or two.

sections.h: Bridging the gaps
p: If a student is below the starting line, do not wait. Plan a short bridging programme in the first six weeks. For sentence mechanics, give a mini-lesson with a one-page rules sheet and five minutes of correction practice at the start of each lesson. For reading, give short graded texts that build from 100 to 200 words, with Who, What, Where, When questions. For listening, practise following simple instructions in class routines. For speaking, use pair talk with sentence starters so that students gain confidence.

Use buddy systems: a stronger student helps a weaker one. Give extra practice for homework and keep it small, so it feels possible. Review progress after three weeks. If a student still cannot reach the baseline after six weeks, talk to your head of department about extra support or a more suitable course.

ex.t: Example: a six-week bridging plan for sentence mechanics
b: Weeks 1 to 2: capital letters, full stops and question marks.
Weeks 3 to 4: simple subject-verb agreement (he plays, they play).
Weeks 5 to 6: simple past tense and linking words and, but, because.
Check with a short writing task each fortnight.

sections.h: Be fair and kind when you find gaps
p: Students may feel shy or ashamed when they find they are behind. Tell them clearly that the diagnostic is not for marks, and that every student has strengths and needs. Do not read out results. Give private feedback. Also look for other reasons for weak results: a new language at home, interrupted schooling, hearing or sight problems, dyslexia or anxiety. If you suspect a special need, speak to your exams officer or SENCO early, because access arrangements need evidence collected over time.
Remember that Cambridge looks for inclusion: the curriculum should help all learners reach their potential. A student who starts behind can still do well with the right support.

ex.t: Example: what to say to a student
b: 'This test shows me where to help you. It does not decide your grade.'
'You are good at... and we will work on...'
'Here is one thing to practise this week.'

units.title: Initial Assessment: Building and Using a Diagnostic Test
units.summary: Design a 30-minute diagnostic test in the style of the exam, mark it with a simple guide, and use the results to adjust your plan.

sections.h: What is an initial assessment?
p: An initial assessment, or baseline test, is given in the first week or two of the course. It is not graded for a report card. It is a diagnostic tool, like a doctor's check-up, used to find weaknesses early so you can change your medium-term plan. It also tells you what students are good at, so you can build on it.

A good diagnostic looks like the real exam tasks but is shorter and simpler. It tests reading, writing and speaking (and, if you have time, listening). Keep it low stress. Tell students it will help you teach them better.

b: Diagnostic: early, short, no grade, used to plan teaching.
Mock exam: later, full length, exam conditions, used to predict and practise.
Do both, but do not mix their purposes.

sections.h: The 30-minute template: Part 1, Vocabulary and Reading (15 minutes)
p: Give students a short blog post of about 150 words about hobbies. Ask them to find three specific facts and explain the meaning of two words used in the text. This checks R1 (specific facts) and whether they can work out vocabulary from context.

Sample text (written for this course): 'My name is Ada and I am fifteen. In my free time I love painting. I started painting two years ago, when my aunt gave me a box of colours for my birthday. Now I paint every Saturday morning in the garden, and sometimes my little brother joins me. Last month I entered a school competition and won second prize, which made me very proud. I also enjoy reading adventure stories, but I am rather busy during the week because of homework. My dream is to hold an exhibition of my pictures when I am older.' Questions: 1. How old is Ada? (fifteen) 2. When does she paint? (every Saturday morning) 3. What did she win? (second prize in a school competition) 4. What does 'proud' mean? 5. What does 'exhibition' mean? Key: students may explain meanings in their own words, for example proud means very happy about something you did; exhibition means a show where pictures are displayed.

b: Questions 1 to 3: 2 marks each (one for the right fact, one for clear, correct writing).
Questions 4 and 5: 2 marks each for a good meaning, 1 mark for a partly correct meaning.
Total 10. Note common errors: copying whole sentences, missing the question word.

sections.h: Part 2: Expressive Writing (15 minutes)
p: Give a simple, prompt-driven task: 'Write an email to a friend telling them about your favourite movie. Write 60 to 80 words.' This is shorter than the exam task, but it checks the same skills. What are you checking? Are they using punctuation correctly? Do they have enough vocabulary to express an opinion? Do they organise ideas in a logical order? Do they use a friendly style?
Do not correct on the page during the test. After the test, mark with a simple rubric (see the next section) and write a short note on each student's profile.

ex.t: Things to notice in the writing
b: Capital letters and full stops.
Subject-verb agreement and verb tenses.
Linking words such as and, but, because.
Whether the student gives a reason and an example.
Greeting and closing suitable for a friend.

sections.h: Part 3: Interactive Speaking Check (5 minutes per student)
p: Have a casual, unscripted chat with each student. Start with: 'Tell me about what you like to do on weekends.' Use follow-up questions such as 'Why do you like that?' and 'What did you do last weekend?' What are you checking? Can they speak without long, painful pauses? Is their pronunciation understandable? Can they answer in more than one word? You can do the speaking checks in pairs while others do written work.

Take brief notes using the four Speaking criteria from the syllabus: grammar, vocabulary, development of answers and pronunciation. You do not need to give marks, but you can give a level from 1 to 5 for each criterion to compare with later in the year.

b: Grammar (1 to 5): ___  Vocabulary (1 to 5): ___
Development (1 to 5): ___  Pronunciation (1 to 5): ___
One strength: ______  One need: ______

sections.h: A simple scoring guide (rubric)
p: Writing (email, 60 to 80 words), total 10 marks. Content, 0 to 4: 4 means all points covered with a reason and an example; 3 means covered with some development; 2 means partly covered; 1 means very little relevant content. Language, 0 to 6: 5 to 6 means mostly accurate with some variety and linking words; 3 to 4 means understandable with some errors and simple structures; 1 to 2 means errors often make meaning hard to follow.

Speaking, levels 1 to 5 for each criterion. Level 5: clear, developed, mostly accurate, easy to follow. Level 4: mostly clear and developed with small errors. Level 3: understandable, simple answers, some support needed. Level 2: very short answers and frequent errors. Level 1: only single words or phrases. This is a classroom tool inspired by the syllabus criteria and is not an official Cambridge scale. Use the official Cambridge descriptors for real Speaking marking later in the course.

ex.t: Example: a student profile after the diagnostic
b: Reading: 7 out of 10 (finds facts well; weaker on word meaning).
Writing: Content 3, Language 3 (needs linking words and verb endings).
Speaking: Grammar 3, Vocabulary 3, Development 2, Pronunciation 4.
Plan: word meaning from context; linking words; speaking expansion.

sections.h: Analyse the class and adjust your plan
p: After marking, make a class table with one row per student and columns for Reading, Writing and Speaking. Colour weak results red and strong results green. Look at the class pattern. If most students are weak in writing language, add more writing practice to Module 1. If a few students are very weak, plan small-group support. If a few are very strong, plan extension tasks, such as longer texts.

Write a short learner profile for each student with one strength, one need for each skill and one goal for the term. File it, and return to it at the end of each term. Students who see their own progress become more responsible and engaged, which are two of the Cambridge learner attributes.

b: Most students lose marks on linking words: add a 10-minute linking-word starter to every writing lesson.
Several students cannot find word meaning from context: teach the context-clue strategy in week 2.
Two students speak very little: use pair work and sentence starters.
Revisit with a short check after six weeks.

sections.h: Share, review and refine your test
p: A good test improves when others look at it. Share your 30-minute diagnostic with two colleagues, and look at theirs. Ask these questions: Are the reading texts too hard for an entry-level student? Is the writing prompt clear? Is the time right? Are the questions testing what we want to test, or only testing difficult vocabulary? Leave short, kind comments and use the advice to improve your test.

In this course platform the document uploader and comments tools may not yet be available. If you cannot upload, share your test by email or in a staff meeting, and keep a note of the feedback you received and the changes you made.

b: Reading text: right length (about 150 words) and level?
Questions: clear, one skill at a time?
Writing prompt: clear purpose, reader and word count?
Speaking questions: friendly, open, not too hard at the start?
Scoring guide: easy to use in under 5 minutes per student?

units.title: My Learning Tracker: Updating Your KWL Chart
units.summary: Use a KWL chart (Know, Want to know, Learned) to track your own professional learning, and write your Week 3 entry.

sections.h: What is a KWL chart?
p: A KWL chart is a three-column organiser that helps you track your own learning journey through this course. K means What I Know, written on Day 1. W means What I Want to know, also written on Day 1. L means What I Learned, filled in at the end of each week. The chart shows you how far you have come, and what you still want to learn.

Reflection is at the heart of the Cambridge teacher. Cambridge says teachers are themselves learners who build their practice through a cycle of reflection, research, evaluation and adaptation. A KWL chart is a simple way to practise that cycle.

b: K (What I Know): filled out on Day 1.
W (What I Want to know): filled out on Day 1.
L (What I Learned): filled out at the end of each week.

sections.h: Your Week 3 entry
p: Open your own notebook, document or journal and update the L column for Week 3. Write at least two new facts you learned this week about balancing long-term plans and checking learner readiness. Be specific. Instead of 'I learned about planning', write 'I learned that I should plan new lessons for only 30 to 32 weeks and keep 6 to 8 weeks for past papers and revision.'

Then check your W column. Did this week answer any of your questions? Cross them out and write the answer. Add any new questions that came up. In this version of the course there is no built-in digital journal yet, so keep your chart on paper or in a document you can find easily.

b: Learned: Cambridge suggests about 130 guided learning hours for an IGCSE subject.
Learned: a diagnostic test should be short, ungraded and used to plan.
Learned: students should enter at a strong A2 to lower B1 level.
Question I still have: how do I plan for mixed-level classes?

sections.h: Reflect on your thinking
p: Look back at your Week 1 K column. How has your understanding of long-term planning changed now that you know you must leave a 6 to 8 week buffer at the end of the year? Write three sentences. What will you do differently this term? Who will you tell?

Good reflection includes what worked, what did not, what you will change and what you need help with. Practise with these four questions each week. After a few weeks, reflection becomes a habit, and habit builds expertise.

b: What worked?
What did not work?
What will I change?
What help do I need?

sections.h: Week 3 checklist
p: Before you move on, tick each item. I have drawn a year map with an exam buffer. I have written a four-column scheme of work for one theme. I know the four baseline skills students need. I have built a diagnostic test with a scoring guide. I have updated my KWL chart. I have shared my work with a colleague and written down one change.

If you cannot tick an item, go back to that unit. These plans are the base of your teaching for the whole year. Next, in Weeks 4 and 5, you will turn the plans into daily lessons and teaching strategies for each skill.

Only the best candidates need a recording
questions.why: The test must be recorded in full for all candidates.

questions.q: Which is NOT a Speaking marking criterion?
questions.why: The four criteria are grammar, vocabulary, development and pronunciation.

questions.q: Which feedback is most helpful to a student?
o: A long list of every error
Two or three specific targets linked to a skill and an action
questions.why: Specific, limited targets with actions help students improve.

questions.q: What is the aim of a standardisation meeting?
questions.why: Standardisation creates consistent marking.

questions.q: A student writes a very long email far above the word range. What is likely?
o: Accuracy and control may suffer, and length alone earns no extra marks
questions.why: Marks are for relevance, development and control of language, not length.

questions.q: What is a distractor in multiple choice?
o: A wrong option that looks attractive
questions.why: Distractors may use words from the text but give the wrong meaning.

questions.q: In the Cambridge guide, what is the 'experienced curriculum'?
o: What learners actually receive from the whole school experience, planned and unplanned
questions.why: The experienced curriculum is what learners really experience, including planned and unplanned outcomes.

questions.q: Which describes a 'spiral approach' to learning?
o: Each stage returns to key ideas and builds on them
Teaching each topic once and never returning
questions.why: In a spiral, learners revisit key learning areas at each stage.

questions.q: According to Cambridge, which is more important when planning a curriculum?
questions.why: Too much content leaves no time for deep understanding. Less can be more.

questions.q: Who writes the schemes of work and lesson plans that make a Cambridge syllabus locally relevant?
questions.why: Cambridge says schools must create their own schemes of work and lessons.

questions.q: How are Cambridge examiners asked to treat spelling and grammar in subjects that are not language tests?
o: Learners are not penalised for spelling and grammar errors
questions.why: Examiners use positive marking and do not penalise spelling and grammar except in tests of language skills.

questions.q: Which is the correct age guidance for Cambridge Lower Secondary?
questions.why: Lower Secondary is for ages 11 to 14.

questions.q: Which grades does Cambridge IGCSE normally award?
questions.why: IGCSE is graded A* to G (and 9 to 1 in some subjects and zones). O Level is A* to E.

questions.q: What is an AS Level?
o: Half the content of an A Level, normally completed in one year
questions.why: An AS Level contains half the content of the corresponding A Level.

questions.q: Which statement about tiers is correct for the 2024 to 2026 IGCSE ESL (0510) syllabus used in this course?
o: It has Core and Extended tiers
It has no tiers: all candidates take the same papers
questions.why: The 2024 to 2026 syllabus removed tiering. Check the syllabus for your exam year.

questions.q: On the CEFR scale, which levels are described as 'independent user'?
questions.why: A is basic, B is independent, C is proficient.

questions.q: About how many guided learning hours are recommended for a Cambridge IGCSE subject?
questions.why: Cambridge suggests about 130 hours per IGCSE or O Level subject.

questions.q: Which is a problem of very short lesson periods, according to the guide?
o: Lessons can become dominated by whole-class teaching
questions.why: There is a tendency for shorter periods to be dominated by whole-class instruction.

questions.q: What does CLIL stand for?
questions.why: CLIL: content and language integrated learning.

questions.q: What did Vygotsky call the area just beyond what a learner can do alone but can do with help?
questions.why: Teachers scaffold learning within this zone.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the five Cambridge learner attributes?
questions.why: The five are confident, responsible, reflective, innovative and engaged.

questions.q: According to the guide, how should ICT be used in the classroom?
o: To support carefully planned teaching and learning goals, not replace them
questions.why: Technology must enhance planned goals, not replace them.

questions.q: How many weeks should be used for new lessons in a 36 to 40 week school year?
questions.why: Leave the last 6 to 8 weeks as an exam buffer.

questions.q: What is a thematic module?
o: A 4 to 6 week block built around one popular topic
questions.why: Modules group about 4 to 6 weeks around a theme such as travel or health.

questions.q: Which column is NOT in the medium-term scheme of work described in this course?
questions.why: The four columns are theme and timeline, language focus, exam skill focus and assessment goal.

questions.q: Which of these is a good learning target?
o: I can write a magazine article with a clear introduction and conclusion
questions.why: A learning target says what the student will be able to do.

questions.q: Which CEFR range should students ideally have when starting IGCSE ESL?
questions.why: Strong A2 to lower B1 is the suggested entry level.

questions.q: Which is an example of a sentence mechanics problem?
questions.why: Subject-verb agreement is part of sentence mechanics.

questions.q: Which best describes the initial assessment?
o: A short ungraded diagnostic used to spot weaknesses early
questions.why: It is a diagnostic tool, not graded for a report card.

questions.q: In the 30-minute template, how long is the writing part?
questions.why: Part 1 is 15 minutes, Part 2 writing is 15 minutes and Part 3 speaking is 5 minutes per student.

questions.q: After the diagnostic, what should you do first?
o: Give the same lesson to everyone
Look for patterns across the class and adjust the plan
questions.why: Results are for planning and support, not ranking.

questions.q: In a KWL chart, what does the W column stand for?
questions.why: K is what I know, W is what I want to know and L is what I learned.
